In particular, we adapt the memory bank based PatchCore algorithm to a federated setting, resulting in increased cold-start performance, resilience to domain- and sensor-shift, and resilience to unreliable actor participation, a common problem in classical, network based federated learning strategies.

title: HILO: Enabling Low-power, Dual-Band Communication using Tunnel Diode Oscillators
comment: 6 pages, 12 figures. Accepted at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on RFID (IEEE RFID 2026)
summary: Wireless communication remains the most power-consuming operation in embedded systems. Low-power transmitters such as backscatter achieve microwatt-scale operation but produce weak signals susceptible to in-band interference and frequency-selective fading, particularly in non-line-of-sight settings. Multi-band transmission can mitigate these effects through spectral-domain redundancy rather than temporal-domain redundancy, improving reliability without sacrificing bitrate or latency. However, conventional multi-band radio transceivers require duplicated RF chains or power-hungry synthesizers. We introduce HILO, a tunnel diode-based frontend that enables dual-band operation from a single circuit. HILO inverts the conventional paradigm: rather than suppressing the harmonics inherent to tunnel diode nonlinearity, it harnesses them. An external device injection-locks the oscillator to a fundamental frequency, simultaneously stabilizing a higher harmonic and yielding two injection-locked carriers without a second oscillator or frequency multiplier. In transmit mode, HILO exploits self-oscillating mixing to modulate both carriers simultaneously; in receive mode, it uses autodyne downconversion at both frequencies. By turning an inherent nonlinearity into a feature, HILO achieves dual-band links while consuming under 210 $μ$W.

title: Does Failure Feedback Direct Agent Self-Modification?
comment: 28 pages, 8 figures, 8 tables. Code, derived data and a script that rederives every number in the paper are included as ancillary files
summary: Self-improving agents use failure feedback to revise their code or instructions, but gains after selection do not establish target-specific repair or generalization. We measure directedness by comparing repair of a randomly selected target failure with repair of the parent's other failures. Across 145 eligible modifications in public Darwin Gödel Machine logs, we find no detectable target-specific advantage. Controlled instruction-revision experiments with small open models show that relevant feedback can improve target repair. In a second study with a pre-specified analysis plan, target feedback raised repair by 20 percentage points for Qwen3-4B relative to matched same-category feedback; the 7-point increase for Phi-4-mini was not significant. Target repair did not reliably imply held-out improvement. Held-out gains were concentrated in settings with identifiable, repairable failure mechanisms, including planted errors and natural tool-interface failures. Benefits of edit localization and regression screening varied across settings, while eight-step revision loops and GEPA ended at similar mean held-out accuracy. Evaluations should report target repair, transfer to related failures, and held-out net change separately.

title: Computing All-Pairs Shortest Communication Time Paths for Periodically Varying Satellite Networks
summary: We address the problem of designing an efficient algorithm for computing the all-pairs shortest-time paths in time-varying networks, specifically targeting the dynamic topological characteristics of low earth orbit (LEO) satellite constellations. We model such temporal graphs as $G = (V, E_t)$, where $V=\{1, 2,\ldots , n\}$ is the set of $n$ vertices in the graph, and $E_t$ is the set of $M$ time-varying edges considered over a total time window of size $T = Mτ$, $τ$ being the duration of each interval in that time window. For such a network, our algorithm finds the all-pair shortest paths in $O(M^2n^3)$-time. A key advantage of our approach is its computational structure, which mirrors two matrix multiplication steps, first in the forward direction and then in the backward direction. This structure of the algorithm makes it exceptionally suitable for parallelization on SIMD architectures like GPUs, thereby offering a significant speedup over traditional shortest-path algorithms and enabling efficient, network-wide message routing in rapidly changing LEO satellite constellations.

title: Revisiting Fast Tendermint: An Agreement Violation and Two Repairs
summary: Fast Tendermint reduces Tendermint's good-case latency to two communication steps for n>=5f+1. We show that its published round-change rule violates Agreement: one Byzantine process suffices for every f>=1, and for f>=2 two Byzantine processes suffice without double signing. The failure occurs when a process advances past a round without recording the value that may have been decided there. The Quint specification that accompanies the protocol does not allow this kind of round skipping and is not affected; the violation lies in the published pseudocode. We present two repairs. Walk requires a process to leave each round on a quorum of that round's precommits and to precommit before leaving. It keeps the recorded valid state and removes the wait after a precommit quorum. Justify carries the evidence needed to accept a proposal in the proposal itself, removing both the recorded valid state and the proposer's synchronization wait. Both satisfy Agreement and Validity under asynchrony and Termination under the partially synchronous gossip model of Tendermint and Fast Tendermint. Both retain proposal timeouts. The main text presents the executions that violate Agreement and explains the two repairs. The appendices provide proofs, a brief comparison with other round-change designs, and an extension to chains.

title: TileCas: Cascading Kernel Development Across Programming Abstractions
comment: 25 pages, 7 figures
summary: Programming abstractions have traditionally been designed for humans, but code generation is increasingly performed by models and autonomous agents. We investigate abstractions for machine-driven programming through GPU and AI-accelerator kernel generation. High-level domain-specific languages (DSLs) simplify search by delegating implementation details to compilers, while lower-level representations provide finer-grained control at the cost of a larger and more complex search space. In this paper, we present TileCas, a unified, pluggable interface that enables coding agents to develop kernels across multiple editable abstraction levels. Rather than committing to a single representation, TileCas allows an agent to transfer and refine candidates across levels through Cross-Level Diagnosis, which maps correctness and performance feedback to actionable controls at different abstraction levels; Abstraction Scheduling, which selects both the candidate and representation from which subsequent refinement should proceed; and a Heterogeneous Search Tree, which preserves and revisits alternative search trajectories spanning multiple representations. We integrate TileCas with two code agents AKO and KDA, and evaluate both integrations on 50 end-to-end KernelBench Level 3 workloads across two accelerator platforms and two language models. Giving equal weight to the four accelerator-model configurations, AKO with TileCas achieves an arithmetic-mean speedup of $4.84\times$, compared with $3.75\times$ for the strongest evaluated baseline without TileCas, an improvement of 29.0%. Integrating the same interface with KDA improves its mean speedup by 69.2%, with gains in every configuration. These results show that allowing coding agents to navigate across programming abstractions can improve machine-driven software development and can be reused across different base workflows.

title: What Is the Cost of a Handover Interruption? Rethinking 5G Mobility for Aerial Vehicles
summary: Low-altitude aviation is moving toward large-scale operations increasingly dependent on 5G cellular connectivity. However, 5G mobility remains blind to the operational risk of its decisions: the same interruption may be harmless in cruise over an empty field but critical near obstacles, crowds or other aircraft. Although 5G already provides mechanisms to obtain location, population density, and radio conditions, mobility decisions do not translate this information into an operational risk metric. We propose Risk-Aware Mobility (RAM), which maps predicted communication disruptions to an operational-risk proxy using information staleness, position uncertainty, and operational context, and exposes this risk to existing mobility mechanisms. In a dense São Paulo deployment with 188 licensed 5G sectors, risk-aware handover timing reduces the mean operational-risk proxy by 45\% relative to conventional A3 without degrading serving-link quality. These results motivate shifting 5G mobility from optimizing handover performance to managing the operational risk of mobility decisions. Beyond handover timing, this perspective raises a broader question: which cells should serve aerial operations when connectivity is evaluated by operational risk rather than radio performance alone?

title: Prorsa: Unleashing the Potential of Prefill-Decode Disaggregation in Agentic Reinforcement Learning
summary: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) is commonly used to enhance the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) in solving complex multi-turn tasks. During rollout, agentic RL exhibits a workload pattern distinct from that of traditional RL: multi-turn interactions repeatedly introduce prefill requests, causing prefill and decode workloads to coexist throughout rollout. This workload makes prefill-decode (PD) disaggregation, a design widely used for online LLM serving, promising for speeding up agentic RL rollout. This paper shows that PD disaggregation can improve rollout efficiency by (a) mitigating interference among data-parallel attention modules, (b) enabling stage-specific parallelism, and (c) reducing end-to-end trajectory completion time. However, a fixed prefill-decode allocation may fail to sustain these benefits as workload composition varies across tasks and over time. We therefore present Prorsa, an agentic RL framework for prediction-guided prefill-decode resource allocation. Prorsa observes the lifecycle of every trajectory to forecast short-horizon prefill and decode demand. These forecasts then guide worker allocation decisions and trigger role switching of rollout engines, aligning prefill and decode capacity with anticipated workload demand. Across synchronous and asynchronous agentic RL settings, Prorsa achieves end-to-end rollout speedups of 1.11x-4.05x over prefill-decode colocation.

title: Do Modifications Made by Coding Agents Make Subsequent Software Maintenance Harder?
summary: Coding agents increasingly maintain repositories over time, where each change becomes the starting point for subsequent tasks. Yet existing benchmarks either start tasks from developer-written code or cannot separate later-task difficulty from the effects of an agent's earlier changes. We ask whether agent-written code makes subsequent maintenance harder and whether the cost stems from inherited test failures or the code itself. We introduce SWE-Maintain, comprising 100 three-event maintenance episodes from 50 real-world Python repositories, with hidden tests certified across each sequence. Each later task is evaluated twice with the same agent and tests: from the developers' preceding patches (Developer-History) and from the agent's own changes (Agent-History). Across five coding systems, two backbone models, and 1,996 paired later events, Agent-History reduces later-task resolution by 5.6 percentage points on average. When success additionally requires all earlier tests to pass, the gap reaches 14.0 points. Two-thirds of Agent-History starting repositories already fail earlier tests, and only 1.9% of events starting from those states end with all accumulated tests passing. When the inherited code passes earlier tests and the next task is not already solved, the disadvantage disappears (+2.7 points; 95% CI [-0.5, +6.1]). These findings suggest that the main downstream cost of agent-written changes lies in inherited test failures rather than a measurable maintenance disadvantage in code that preserves earlier tested behavior. Evaluations should therefore include agent-produced history, and coding agents should preserve earlier behavior across changes.

title: QoE-Aware Service Function Chain Orchestration in Space-Air-Ground Integrated Networks for In-Flight Internet
comment: 13 pages, 10 figures
summary:
In remote regions lacking terrestrial infrastructure, aviation users increasingly demand Internet services comparable to ground cellular networks. This paper proposes a space-air-ground integrated network (SAGIN) architecture that combines ground networks, civil aviation networks, and low Earth orbit (LEO) satellites. Based on real North Atlantic flight data, a heterogeneous aviation Internet is constructed to support diverse aircraft service requirements.
  A composite Quality of Experience (QoE) metric, characterized by transmission delay, jitter, and content similarity, guides efficient resource utilization. The dynamic connectivity of SAGIN is modeled using a reconfigurable time-expanded graph (RTEG). With Network Function Virtualization (NFV), data delivery is formulated as a Service Function Chain (SFC) deployment across ground stations, relay aircraft, and satellites, resulting in a long-term QoE maximization problem.
  A tailored Multi-Agent Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (MADDPG) algorithm incorporating LCSS-based path filtering and softmax-based action selection is developed. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed approach enables seamless connectivity for heterogeneous aircraft and consistently outperforms game-theoretic and MATD3 methods in terms of QoE.

title: StageBreaker: Shifting Video RL Post-Training Scheduling from Stages down to Data Dependencies
comment: 16 pages, 16 figures
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training has emerged as the key paradigm for improving autoregressive video models. Emerging vision-language reward models further strengthen post-training with accurate rewards, but their long chain-of-thought inference substantially raises the associated costs, while the pursuit of long videos prolongs policy training. Despite these rising costs, existing video RL systems still adopt coarse-grained stage-centric execution, which stalls policy training until all reward evaluation finishes, replays every trajectory twice due to a further barrier within policy training, and induces load imbalance across GPUs. To address the challenges, we propose StageBreaker, a fine-grained data-dependency-driven scheduling framework, which schedules the true dataflow of an RL step rather than its stages. Specifically, StageBreaker overlaps policy training with reward evaluation by exploiting reward-separable policy training, and merges the two trajectory replays into one by leveraging loss-independent back-propagation. It further balances GPU load by scheduling computation at the finer granularity. Our evaluation results show that StageBreaker achieves a speedup of up to 1.41$\times$ over stage-centric execution.

title: Testuary: Agentic Test Generation with Zero-Shot Parallelism
summary: Agentic approaches for automated test generation can reach high-quality results, but they improve a given test suite incrementally, so a weak starting point may lead to many iterations or insufficient tests. To address this, we present Testuary, which provides the agentic phases with an improved starting point. Testuary first generates multiple test suites through independent, parallel zero-shot requests, checks and repairs them deterministically, and combines them into a single suite with a novel structural merging approach. A runtime-weighted set-cover reduction removes redundant tests without losing covered lines, branches, or killed mutants. After that, two agentic phases target the remaining gaps in coverage and mutation score. We compare Testuary with established search and LLM-based test generation approaches. The non-agentic first phase alone already significantly outperforms the current state-of-the-art. After the agentic phases, Testuary achieves on average more than 99.9% line and branch coverage as well as a mutation score of 98.6%, significantly outperforming all compared baseline approaches. Testuary needs fewer model requests and its test suites are on average smaller and faster than those of the compared agentic approach.

title: Towards Virtual Networking for a Time-Triggered Hypervisor
comment: Published at RTNS 2025. This is the author's version of the work
summary: Virtualization enables mixed-criticality applications to run on shared hardware by isolating them within separate virtual machines (VMs). However, achieving end-to-end timing guarantees for critical tasks hosted on virtual CPUs (VCPUs) without relying on static partitioning is hard. A possible solution is a time-triggered hypervisor that dispatches VMs' VCPUs to processor cores according to a predetermined global schedule. A global schedule includes the computation, the network, and the virtualization layer to provide end-to-end timing guarantees across hosts and VMs during design time. In this work, we propose a VirtIO-based virtual network that realizes IEEE 802.1Qbv quasi-compliant inter-VM communication, providing predictable timing for critical messages exchanged between time-triggered VMs. We present our VirtIO-based virtual network architecture and derive network-level scheduling constraints that emerge from the properties of the proposed solution. We implement the proposed design in the ACRN hypervisor and evaluate the end-to-end latency of critical traffic in a loaded network, demonstrating that our time-triggered VirtIO-net prototype provides predictable end-to-end latency under load.

title: Improved Massively Parallel Shortest Path Computation
summary:
We present new algorithms for approximate shortest path computation in weighted undirected graphs within the Massively Parallel Computation (MPC) model. Specifically, we construct an $a$-approximate Single-Source Shortest Path (SSSP) oracle: Given a query consisting of a source vertex $u \in V$, the oracle returns $a$-approximate distances $δ(u,v)$ for all $v \in V$.
  Fix an $n$-vertex weighted undirected graph. We consider two regimes of the MPC model: the near-linear regime, where each machine has $\tildeΘ(n)$ memory, and the heterogeneous regime, where all machines have $Θ(n^γ)$ memory for some constant $γ\in (0,1]$, except for a single machine with $\tildeΘ(n)$ memory. We develop randomised algorithms that construct $O(1)$-approximate SSSP oracles in $O(\log\log n)$ rounds in the near-linear regime and in $O(\log^2\log n)$ rounds in the heterogeneous regime. These oracles answer distance queries in $O(1)$ rounds. Our results improve upon the recent work of Dory and Matar (SPAA 2024) which, for the same total memory, requires $\left(\log\log n\right)^{2+O(1/γ)}$ rounds and applies only to unweighted graphs in the heterogeneous setting.
  We say that $\tilde N_k(u)$ is the approximate $k$-nearest neighbourhood of a vertex $u$ if there exists an approximate distance estimate $δ$ such that $\tilde N_k(u)$ consists of the $k$ vertices closest to $u$ according to $δ$, breaking ties by vertex ID. The main technical ingredient is a new method for efficiently computing approximate $n^{O(γ)}$-nearest neighbourhoods in the heterogeneous MPC model in $O(\log^2\log n)$ rounds.

title: AI-Native Product Management: A Vision
summary: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to support product management tasks. At the same time, AI-native research and development (R&D) may increase software realization capacity. Organizations may realize software faster than they can identify, qualify, and reconsider what should be realized. This paper asks how product management should be re-envisioned under these conditions. We synthesize research on software product management, product learning, human-AI collaboration, and the Product Management and R&D boundary. We propose a vision in which AI becomes a persistent participant in product work. The vision covers sensing, exploration, decision-making, realization, and learning. We propose six principles and make the vision tangible through an operating model grounded in human professionals, AI personas, agents, skills, and a shared product context. We further argue that AI-native Product Management and AI-native R&D can form a continuous product-learning process. Finally, we identify four AI-specific research directions that require empirical investigation.

title: Shortcut in Generalization: Rethinking Evaluation Protocol for Encrypted Traffic Classification
comment: Accepted for publication at IEEE CSCloud 2026
summary: Encrypted traffic classification is commonly evaluated under a range of experimental protocols, with classification performance reported as the primary measure. However, the reported performance may be influenced by shortcuts left uncontrolled in the evaluation protocol, such as shortcut features and cross-partition sharing, rather than reflect generalizable traffic patterns. And test-only feature transformations may further introduce train-test mismatch. In this paper, we study how current evaluation protocols are affected by shortcut-related factors, including field-level shortcuts, cross-partition sharing, and train-test processing. We compare feature importance, retrained feature removal, and field-only split sensitivity. We also vary Source-IP overlap and packets per flow, compare test-only IP transformations with matched train-test transformations. Experiments on three public datasets show that the performance of existing methods are affected by both cross-partition sharing and the consistency of train-test transformations. Specifically, increasing Source-IP overlap from 0% to 100% raises accuracy by about 32-33 points before identifier masking, compared with only about 8 points after masking. For two state-of-the-art pretrained models (i.e., YaTC and NetMamba), the 11-13 points loss caused by test-only IP zeroing is almost fully recovered when the same transformation is applied during both training and testing.

title: Beyond the Boundary: Optimal Grid Dispersion by Spread, Reverse, and Collect
summary: \emph{Dispersion} requires a set of mobile agents to occupy distinct nodes of a graph such that each node contains at most one agent. We study deterministic dispersion of $k\le n$ agents on an $n$-node oriented square grid, where each node has globally consistent North, East, South, and West port labels, from arbitrary initial configurations. This includes both \emph{rooted} configurations, where all agents are co-located initially, and \emph{general} configurations, where agents are initially distributed arbitrarily across the nodes. On oriented square grids, Kshemkalyani, Molla, and Sharma~\cite{KMS20} gave an $O(\min(k,\Side))$-round algorithm in the local-communication model, where only agents on the same node can exchange information, and an $O(\sqrt{k})$-round algorithm in the global-communication model, where any two agents can communicate regardless of position, both using $O(\log k)$ bits per agent. The bound in the local communication model is optimal when $k=Θ(n)$, but it remains open whether local communication alone can match the $Ω(\sqrt{k})$ time lower bound when $k=o(n)$. We solve this by presenting \textsc{Spread--Reverse--Collect} (SRC), a deterministic algorithm that disperses any $k\le n$ agents in $O(\sqrt{k})$ synchronous rounds using $O(\log k)$ bits of persistent memory per agent, matching both time and memory lower bounds. SRC is based on a geometric primitive, a \sharpS-shaped parallel sweep, together with a simple priority rule. Unlike earlier grid algorithms that gather agents at the boundary and spread out from there, each SRC sweep starts from the agents' current position, and when it reaches the boundary the group simply reflects its sweep back inside and continues. SRC therefore needs no knowledge of the grid size and runs unchanged on an infinite oriented grid.

title: Humans vs. Machines: A Comparison With AI Agents in Software Reverse Engineering
summary: Can an autonomous AI agent reverse engineer a binary as well as a skilled human analyst? Do they adopt the same strategy, and can agents scale to real-world programs? We compare human and LLM-based software reverse engineering (SRE): nine models tackle two compact static-analysis challenges previously solved by human analysts, scored with a common understanding rubric, and we record their complete interactions with IDA Pro. This lets us compare not only what humans and agents recover, but also how they investigate a binary. The best agents (GPT-5.5 Pro, Claude Opus 4.8, and Kimi K3) achieve statistically human-competitive understanding on both tasks, while weaker models remain far behind. Ablations show that the gap depends on code representation and workflow demands, not on model capability alone: open-weight models improve substantially with richer code representations, whereas frontier models show no significant change. Similar success rates hide different workflows. Humans repeatedly revisit functions and follow local program structure; strong agents jump across the binary, retrieve information broadly, and rarely return to inspected code, a behavior we call greedy fetching. This strategy is not fixed: given semantically richer code, agents fetch less without losing understanding. Because greedy fetching aggregates large amounts of code in the agent's context, we measure context-window saturation across 4,000 real-world binaries: large windows accommodate many programs, but larger applications and lower-level representations quickly exhaust them. Autonomous reverse engineering is becoming competitive, with a large speed advantage, but scaling it will require better navigation, selective retrieval, and persistent analysis state, not merely larger context windows.

title: CALM-5G: Event-Level Conformal Risk Control for Predictive Service-Assurance Alarms
comment: 15 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Network and Service Management
summary: Predictive service assurance converts forecasts of key performance indicators into alarms, and that conversion decides whether the assurance function is deployable. We present CALM-5G, an assurance layer that operates above any forecasting backbone and issues alarms with distribution-free, finite-sample guarantees. It calibrates on service-level violation events, scores violation onset directly, selects its calibration scheme out of sample, and reports the alarm duty cycle with every certified miss rate. Four corpora are evaluated separately, namely a production cellular network, commercial 5G traces, an open radio access network testbed and our 5G standalone testbed. Risk control on the regression-derived score yields duty cycles of 0.24 to 0.91. Onset targeting with cross-validated calibration reduces time-in-alarm by 56.3% to 89.7% on three corpora, with no significant change on the fourth. The realised miss rate stays within a two-standard-error tolerance on three corpora and within one standard error of it on the fourth. Under label shift, pooled batch calibration exceeds that tolerance structurally, by 10.9 standard errors on the production corpus. Online calibration restores compliance. Calibration schemes cannot be ranked on the split that fits their thresholds. Miss rate and duty cycle are certified jointly where within-entity dependence leaves sufficient calibration units.

title: MODAIC: Coordinated Asynchrony for Decentralized Multimodal Learning
summary: Multimodal decentralized learning enables collaboration across heterogeneous edge devices without sharing raw data, but differing modality sets create coupled computation and communication bottlenecks. Multimodal agents support cross-modal alignment while training more model components and sharing bandwidth across multiple modality overlays. Under bandwidth limits, these agents can become hot spots: transfers miss aggregation windows, and their updates become stale or underrepresented, degrading worst-agent accuracy. Asynchrony removes global blocking but does not by itself coordinate local cross-modal interaction with timely peer-update exchange. We present MODAIC (Modality-Decoupled Asynchrony with Interleaved Coordination), a wait-free system that coordinates local modality progress, peer-to-peer update delivery, and aggregation under heterogeneous compute and bandwidth. Hierarchical asynchrony lets modalities progress independently while enforcing reciprocal feature exchange; load-aware update fetching overlaps training with communication, limits concurrent serving load, and reuses late arrivals; and consensus-aware peer selection uses lightweight metadata to account for update availability, peer participation, and loss similarity without active probing. We implement MODAIC as a containerized multi-agent framework and evaluate it on local and cross-region cloud testbeds. Across AVE and KU-HAR, MODAIC improves average accuracy and multimodal worst-agent performance. On AVE at 200 Mbps per agent, it improves multimodal worst-agent accuracy by 11.0 percentage points at 1000 seconds over the strongest baseline. On the cloud testbed, it reduces time-to-accuracy by up to 30%. Ablations show that simpler load-balancing and delayed-aggregation variants leave a worst-agent accuracy gap, and stress tests show tolerance to WAN variability and partial tracker unavailability.

title: TurnCost: Turns, Not Observations: Cache-Aware Loop Engineering for Coding Agents
summary:
AI coding agents operate in iterative loops: they modify code, run tools, inspect the results, and decide what to do next. We call the design of this process loop engineering, which includes context management, model selection, compaction, and termination. Existing efficiency work mainly compresses tool observations or routes selected turns to cheaper models, but the practical opportunity for these optimizations remains unclear. We analyze 600 publicly released coding-agent trajectories spanning two agent scaffolds and two language models. Median observations contain only 118-286 tokens, while the large build logs commonly used to motivate compression occur near the ninety-ninth percentile. Moreover, 98.6% of input tokens are served from a prefix cache, so flat input pricing overestimates loop cost by roughly 7x on average under near-ideal caching.
  We derive and empirically validate a closed-form break-even condition for model delegation. Delegation increases cost in half of the evaluated settings, near the predicted boundary. More broadly, turn count explains 84% of the variance in log trajectory cost, compared with 4% for mean observation size; the most expensive trajectories have the most turns despite having the smallest observations. These associations suggest that observation-focused methods target a secondary cost factor, and identify unnecessary turns as the larger and largely unexamined opportunity, though we do not establish that turns can be removed while holding task success fixed. We release TurnCost, a tool for re-scoring trajectory corpora under alternative caching, pricing, compression, and routing policies.

title: NetCoFi: A Budget-Aware Coarse-Fine Dual-Branch Model for Encrypted Traffic Classification
comment: Accepted for publication at IEEE CSCloud 2026
summary: Encrypted traffic classification is critical for network management and security, but practical deployment must balance classification accuracy and inference cost. Existing models typically process fixed flow windows with limited control over computation after training, which can limit the accuracy-efficiency trade-off under constrained resources. To address this problem, we present NetCoFi, a budget-aware classifier that allocates computation at coarse and fine granularities. Using byte representations and observable packet metadata, NetCoFi selects token neighborhoods for fine-grained encoding while compressing the full window into complementary coarse context. Multi-budget training enables the same model to operate at different routing budgets without retraining. Evaluation on six public datasets shows that NetCoFi achieves state-of-the-art classification performance when trained from scratch. Under low-budget settings, NetCoFi improves average Macro-F1 by 7.86 percentage points across three datasets, compared with a same-depth static baseline. In a DPDK-GPU traffic processing pipeline, it increases mean batch throughput from 26.42 to 43.42 Mb/s, a 1.64x improvement over NetMamba.

title: FlashT2S: GPU-Accelerated Tensor-to-Spike Conversion Operators for Heterogeneous Neuromorphic LLM Backends
summary:
Artificial intelligence faces two growing challenges: computational bottlenecks and energy inefficiency inherent to the von Neumann architecture. Neuromorphic computing offers a promising alternative, yet its immature ecosystem still relies on conventional systems for data supply, requiring efficient conversion between tensor and spike dataflow.
  We observe a clear mismatch, where data conversion is slow while downstream computation is fast. As data size grows quadratically with large language models, this mismatch becomes a major bottleneck.
  In this work, we examine the data-conversion components that appear on the critical path of training and inference in neuromorphic LLMs. The work presents FlashT2S (Flash Tensor-to-Spike): GPU-Accelerated Tensor-to-Spike Conversion Operators, which applies architecture-aware and data-centric optimizations to reduce conversion latency. Experimental results show that FlashT2S delivers an average speedup of 850.78x over the native operators across individual operators and 802.83x in realistic workloads. Additionally, compared with GPU kernels automatically generated by torch.compile, our kernels achieve 5-11x speedups. Notably, it achieves near-optimal absolute performance: large-scale conversions are reduced to tens of microseconds (10-99 us), while small-scale conversions reach single-digit microsecond levels (less than 10 us). Furthermore, its standardized output enables seamless integration across heterogeneous backends, including diverse neuromorphic hardware.

title: Verifying Autoware Controller Node by Combining Model Verification and Runtime Monitoring
comment: 34 pages, 9 figures, 2 tables. Extended version of a paper accepted at SEFM 2026
summary: Formal modeling and verification of autonomous driving systems remain challenging due to the vast operational space and the complexity of the control logic. We propose a hybrid verification approach that combines formal model verification and runtime monitoring for the trajectory-following control node of Autoware, an open-source autonomous driving platform. We formalize the controller as a hybrid system in differential dynamic logic (dL), and introduce an abstract model that captures the essential control dynamics. We then prove safety and liveness properties of the model using the KeYmaera X proof assistant. Complementarily, we monitor the constraints that assure the compatibility between the model and the Autoware implementation across numerical simulation runs using the Autoware toolchain, quantifying to what extent the implementation's behavior is subsumed by the verified model. The experimental results confirmed that (i) monitoring provides a sound evaluation of target following with accuracy bounds, and (ii) the Autoware implementation reaches the target with an accuracy of approximately 0.2-0.4 (m) in position and 0.8 (m/s) in velocity.

title: Developments in Building Towards the Indian SKA Regional Centre
summary: The SKA Regional Centre Network (SRCNet) is a federated global network designed to archive, distribute, and process SKAO data products. This paper examines the evolving SRCNet architecture-focusing on the transition to version 0.2 (v0.2) requirements, including computation, orchestration, and multi-tiered storage-and details the strategy for establishing its proto-SRC infrastructure. We outline the prototype developments for the major and minor nodes in the context of v0.2. We describe the minor node compute and storage demands, establishing a pathway toward a fully operational Indian SKA Regional Centre (INSRC).

title: GPU Goldmines: Tunable WebGPU Kernels for Edge LLM Inference
comment: 11 pages, 5 figures, 5 tables
summary: As demand for LLM inference grows and consumer GPUs grow more capable, edge deployment is becoming increasingly attractive. WebGPU is compelling in this setting because it offers cross-platform portability and browser accessibility. However, these same strengths also make high performance difficult to achieve, as an implementation that performs well in one context may not perform well in another. To address this, we present GPU Goldmines, a framework for specifying, executing, and tuning WebGPU kernels. We instantiate GPU Goldmines with kernels for key LLM building blocks: matrix multiplication, matrix-vector multiplication, and flash attention. We characterize performance across diverse devices, shapes, and browsers, and use the resulting database to accelerate subsequent autotuning and configuration selection. On shapes drawn from Llama and Qwen models, our matrix multiplication kernels outperform ONNX Runtime and llama.cpp WebGPU kernels by 7.0x and 1.41x geometric mean, respectively, and deliver end-to-end improvements of 1.48x in the prefill stage of llama.cpp for chat workloads.

title: PassSum: Leveraging Paths of Abstract Syntax Trees and Self-Supervision for Code Summarization
comment: Journal of Software Evolution and Process, 2024
summary: Code summarization is to provide a high-level comment for a code snippet that typically describes the function and intent of the given code. Recent years have seen the successful application of data-driven code summarization. To improve the performance of the model, numerous approaches use Abstract Syntax Trees (ASTs) to represent the structural information of the code, which is considered by most researchers to be the main factor that distinguishes code from natural language. Then, such data-driven methods are trained on large-scale labeled datasets to obtain a model with strong generalization capabilities that can be applied to new examples. Nevertheless, we argue that state-of-the-art approaches suffer from two key weaknesses: (1) inefficient encoding of ASTs; (2) reliance on a large labeled corpus for model training. As a result, such drawbacks lead to (1) oversized model, slow training, information loss and instability; (2) inability to be applied to programming languages with only a small amount of labeled data. In light of these weaknesses, we propose PassSum, a code summarization approach that addresses the aforementioned weaknesses via (1) a novel input representation which contains an efficient AST encoding method; (2) introducing three pre-training objectives and pre-training our model with a large amount of (easy-to-obtain) unlabeled data under the guidance of self-supervised learning. Experimental results on code summarization for Java, Python and Ruby methods demonstrate the superiority of PassSum to state-of-the-art methods. Further experiments demonstrate that the input representation we use has both temporal and spatial advantages in addition to performance leadership. In addition, pre-training is also shown to make the model more generalizable with less labeled data, and also to speed up the convergence of the model during training.

title: Tanchun: Robust Flow-Based HTTP(S) DDoS Detection via Behavioral Attribute Guidance
summary:
HTTP(S) DDoS attacks have surged in frequency and scale, posing a significant threat to network security. Flow-based detection is a promising solution for large-scale HTTP(S) DDoS detection due to its decryption-free operation and scalability. However, the coarse-grained numerical statistics in flow data limit accurate attack detection and lack robustness when benign and attack traffic patterns drift over time.
  In this paper, we present Tanchun, a drift-aware flow-based HTTP(S) DDoS detection system that relies solely on decryption-free flow data. Specifically, Tanchun groups flows by IP-pair and aggregates them over consecutive time slots into behavior sequences, capturing temporal access patterns to compensate for the limited information in individual flows. It further abstracts these sequences into human-understandable behavioral attributes that capture stable behavioral semantics. Tanchun then aligns behavior sequences with their corresponding behavioral attributes to guide representation learning, enabling robust detection under traffic drift.
  We evaluate Tanchun across diverse HTTP(S) DDoS scenarios. Tanchun achieves the best overall performance, with an average F1-score of 0.988, and outperforms the second-best method by 5.3\% and 9.6\% under benign-traffic and attack-traffic drift, respectively. Experiments on real-world traffic traces further demonstrate its practical effectiveness.

title: ATTUNE: Agentic Throughput Tuning for LLM Training
comment: "21 pages, 2 figures, 14 tables
summary: Training recipes are tuned by hand for one model, cluster and workload, and every new model, accelerator, framework version or dataset means tuning again. Automated tuners search a fixed space of knobs and check only that a job runs, yet a configuration can run to completion while it silently changes training. ATTUNE is a single coding agent that tunes any working recipe for the workload and stack at hand, unattended, within a GPU-hour budget the user sets. It diagnoses each run and changes one lever at a time, guided by a catalog of lessons from past campaigns, and ships a recipe only if it passes a correctness gate: a configuration check against objective-changing settings and known stack defects, and a convergence check of its loss curve against the baseline's. On four held-out models at 64-128 GPUs, ATTUNE raises mean throughput over the strongest public recipe run on our stack by 6.7% on Llama-3.1-405B (best campaign 11.9%) and 33.9% on GLM-4.5 (54.7%), whose public recipe was written for H100. It keeps Mixtral-8x22B's recipe, where nothing it finds clears the noise band. Under a common GPU-hour budget it beats OptiCo, Bayesian optimization and random search on GLM-4.5 and MiniMax-M2; on GLM-4.5 its mean gain is more than four times the best alternative's at less than half the GPU-hours, and on both models its tuning pays for itself within a day of training. The gate rejects no legitimate run and catches 16 of 24 faulty runs, missing only ones that barely move the 20-step loss. Ablations tie its best campaigns to one of its search rules: retrying an out-of-memory layout with recomputation. We release ATTUNE's code and TrainingThroughputBench, a leaderboard of the fastest known recipes for MoE models up to 744B parameters on up to 256 GPUs, each with its throughput, cost per million tokens and a passed correctness check, at https://github.com/amazon-science/attune.

title: Comparing the Pre-trained Models of Source Code by Re-pre-training under a Unified Setup
comment: IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems, 2024
summary: Recent years have seen the successful application of large pre-trained models of source code (CodePTMs) to code representation learning, which have taken the field of software engineering (SE) from task-specific solutions to task-agnostic generic models. By the remarkable results, CodePTMs are seen as a promising direction in both academia and industry. While a number of CodePTMs have been proposed, they are often not directly comparable because they differ in experimental setups such as pre-training dataset, model size, evaluation tasks and datasets, etc. In this paper, we first review the experimental setup used in previous work and propose a standardized setup to facilitate fair comparisons among CodePTMs to explore the impacts of their pre-training tasks. Then, under the standardized setup, we re-pre-train CodePTMs using the same model architecture, input modalities, and pretraining tasks, etc., as they declared and fine-tune each model on each evaluation SE task for evaluating. Finally, we present the experimental results and make a comprehensive discussion on the relative strength and weakness of different pre-training tasks w.r.t. each SE task. We hope our view can inspire and advance the future study of more powerful CodePTMs.

title: An Optical KV Cache Network for Disaggregated LLM Serving
summary: Disaggregated LLM serving moves each request's KV cache from a prefill GPU to a decode GPU before the response begins, and a coding-agent turn often moves the KV of its whole long context. Behind an oversubscribed packet fabric this transfer adds to time to first token (TTFT). An optical circuit switch (OCS) can give every transfer a full-rate circuit for less than an oversubscribed packet fabric costs, but a mechanical OCS needs tens of milliseconds to reconfigure. We hide this delay inside the prefill. A reservation scheduler commits each circuit while the prefill is still computing, so the circuit is ready when the KV is, and each GPU reaches the OCS over its own wavelength-multiplexed (WDM) optics on one fiber pair. In simulations of GPU clusters on real serving traces with measured prefill times on H100 GPUs, this optical KV cache network matches 400G packet fabrics with adaptive routing at 0.55 to 0.78 times the cost of a 2:1 fabric and tolerates the 50 ms reconfiguration delay of a 384-port mechanical OCS.

title: FLAI Protocol: Decentralized Federated Learning with On-Chain Rewards and sPEG-Based Contribution Scoring
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures. Published in Proc. 2026 IEEE International Conference on Consumer Electronics (ICCE). (c) 2026 IEEE
summary: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training without data centralization but struggles with incentive alignment, accountability, and robustness under heterogeneous non-IID data. Existing decentralized FL (DeFL) systems leverage blockchains for coordination yet face high on-chain overhead, unverifiable self-reports, and weak fairness guarantees. We present the FLAI Protocol, a trusted execution environment (TEE)-backed DeFL framework that integrates enclave-validated aggregation, sparse Peer Evaluation Graph (sPEG) scoring, and on-chain settlement. sPEG incorporates peer-based quality, class coverage, promptness, effort, and reputation into composite contribution scores. The protocol formalizes contribution evaluation and tokenized incentive distribution, ensuring verifiable fairness and resilience against free-riding and collusion. We evaluate FLAI on image, text, and healthcare datasets and demonstrate parity with FedAvg in utility while improving fairness and accountability. A case study in consumer eHealth (aggregating wearable and electronic health record data for real-world evidence generation) illustrates the protocol's applicability to privacy-critical domains where equitable rewards, auditability, and data sovereignty are essential.

title: When Messages Go Wrong: Understanding Communication Faults in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
comment: 21 pages, 11 figures, 3 tables. Code and experimental artifacts: https://github.com/SonGoKu21/mas_communication/ ; companion website: https://songoku21.github.io/mas_communication/
summary: LLM-based multi-agent systems (LLM-MAS) use specialized agents that exchange messages to accomplish complex tasks. Their reliance on networked protocols, remote tools, and model endpoints exposes communication to message loss, delay, and context expiration. Because agents often exchange open-ended natural language, anomalies can alter task-relevant information while leaving messages processable, allowing semantic errors to propagate through subsequent interactions. Systematic studies of faults in inter-agent communication remain limited. This paper presents a large-scale empirical study of how communication faults manifest, propagate, and affect task outcomes in LLM-MAS. We construct a cross-layer taxonomy linking lower-stack disturbances to application-visible faults and develop a fault-injection and tracing pipeline. Our evaluation covers more than 29,000 executions across 100 tasks, five domains, three workflow topologies, and three model configurations. We find that 20.7% of failures with complete detection records occur without an immediate failure signal, reaching 76.2% for partial-content faults. Flat maintains 53.0% task success under communication faults, compared with 3.3% and 3.2% for Sequential and Hierarchical, respectively. This advantage primarily arises when an alternative information path preserves the evidence required by downstream agents. We also evaluate execution-side and evidence protection mechanisms and find that they recover different failure cases. Evidence recovery depends on whether trustworthy information remains accessible through an unaffected path. These observations provide empirical insights into communication-fault propagation, workflow resilience, and protection design for LLM-MAS.

title: Pedestrian Trajectory Prediction through LoRA Federated Training
comment: 6 pages, 7 figures, 3 tables, Accepted IEEE Consumer Communications & Networking Conference (CCNC) 2027
summary:
In Intelligent Transport Systems, protecting vulnerable road users, specifically pedestrians, is a paramount challenge. The present work contributes to this field, putting forth a distributed architecture in which vehicles connected to the cellular infrastructure collect pedestrians' trajectories and fine-tune a foundation model for pedestrian trajectory forecasting via federated training. A server positioned at the edge of the cellular network is responsible for aggregating the local model's parameters from the vehicles and updating the global model's parameters. To reduce radio resource utilization, Low-Rank Adaptation is proposed; to decrease both the number and the size of updates, an increase in the number of training rounds performed by the vehicles per communication round is put forth. A novel figure of merit is then introduced to quantify the use of radio resources dedicated to Vehicle-to-Infrastructure communications as required by the federated solution.
  The proposed scheme delivers excellent prediction accuracy while significantly reducing the communication cost compared to alternative federated training methods. This shows that combining fine-tuning, Low-Rank Adaptation, and a reduction of the communication periodicity between the vehicles and the edge server is key to enabling a distributed approach to trajectory prediction in vehicular environments.

title: Capacity over TFLOPS: Memory-Centric Deployment of Large Clinical Language Models on Consumer CPUs
comment: 6 pages, 4 figures. Accepted to the 2026 IEEE 15th International Conference on Consumer Electronics - Berlin (ICCE-Berlin). (c) 2026 IEEE. Code: https://github.com/balkeumlabs/LLM-on-CPU
summary: The dominant barrier to running large clinical language models at the point of care is not arithmetic throughput but graphics memory: consumer GPUs cap at 4-16 GB, while the working set of a 27-billion-parameter model in 4-bit precision is 17-25 GB. We argue that the edge node should be treated as capacity-enabled (system RAM) rather than compute-limited (GPU VRAM), and we test this on commodity hardware. Using an INT4 build of a 27B open model as an architecture-faithful stand-in for a 27B medical model, we measure the memory footprint, inference latency, energy, and federated communication cost of a fully CPU-based pipeline driven by synthetic Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) prompts. On two independent consumer machines (a desktop-class machine with 67 GB of RAM and a 6 GB GPU, and a mobile workstation with 34 GB of RAM and a 4 GB GPU) the model loads entirely into system RAM (37% and 60% utilization, respectively) while both GPUs are out-of-memory before the first step. Inference runs at overnight-batch speed (0.6-2.4 tokens/s for the 27B model), and federated fine-tuning would transmit only a 22.6 MB low-rank adapter, a 99.96% reduction over full weights. The capacity result is independent of CPU microarchitecture, RAM size, operating system, and GPU. We further identify an open, CPU- and NPU-optimized inference runtime as the natural production path for this approach, indicating a privacy-preserving and broadly deployable route for on-premises clinical AI. All data is synthetic; this is a research artifact and not a medical device.

title: Reviewing Beyond the Change: Repository Size and Existing Code Across Agent and Human Pull Requests
comment: 45 pages, 3 figures, 7 tables. Data and code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23290164
summary: Reviewers sometimes name existing repository items outside the change under review. We ask whether such references are more common in larger repositories, and whether the pattern differs between agent-authored and human-authored pull requests. An instrument resolves names in inline review comments against the base-commit repository; size-matched negative controls estimate chance matches. Among 92,042 comments on agent pull requests in 2,034 GitHub repositories, 6.5 per cent name an existing item outside the change. An internally pre-specified log-linear model finds an odds ratio of 1.35 per tenfold increase in code files (interval 1.15 to 1.59), and size-matched negative controls indicate that chance matching does not account for the rise. Exploratory analyses suggest that the association is concentrated from small to mid-sized repositories and is imprecise among large ones. Human pull requests in 1,845 of these repositories show a similar association. A pre-specified comparison finds a small agent excess just within the bound set as negligible, but the evidence does not establish a robust agent-specific difference. The instrument misses many references, so reported shares likely understate prevalence, and the validation cannot estimate how recall changes with repository size.

title: HILO: Enabling Low-power, Dual-Band Communication using Tunnel Diode Oscillators
comment: 6 pages, 12 figures. Accepted at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on RFID (IEEE RFID 2026)
summary: Wireless communication remains the most power-consuming operation in embedded systems. Low-power transmitters such as backscatter achieve microwatt-scale operation but produce weak signals susceptible to in-band interference and frequency-selective fading, particularly in non-line-of-sight settings. Multi-band transmission can mitigate these effects through spectral-domain redundancy rather than temporal-domain redundancy, improving reliability without sacrificing bitrate or latency. However, conventional multi-band radio transceivers require duplicated RF chains or power-hungry synthesizers. We introduce HILO, a tunnel diode-based frontend that enables dual-band operation from a single circuit. HILO inverts the conventional paradigm: rather than suppressing the harmonics inherent to tunnel diode nonlinearity, it harnesses them. An external device injection-locks the oscillator to a fundamental frequency, simultaneously stabilizing a higher harmonic and yielding two injection-locked carriers without a second oscillator or frequency multiplier. In transmit mode, HILO exploits self-oscillating mixing to modulate both carriers simultaneously; in receive mode, it uses autodyne downconversion at both frequencies. By turning an inherent nonlinearity into a feature, HILO achieves dual-band links while consuming under 210 $μ$W.

title: A Minimum Exact Disjunctive Basis for Two-Robot Solvability Profiles
comment: 100 pages, 2 figures, 9 tables
summary:
We completely characterize the solvability profiles of tasks for two autonomous mobile robots in the plane under variable disorientation, chirality, and rigid movements. The four standard capability models and the schedulers considered here have a known quotient order Q of thirteen computational classes. A task's solvability profile is the set of classes in which it is solvable, and is necessarily an upset of Q. We prove that every upset is realizable and construct a minimum exact disjunctive basis of thirteen concrete tasks.
  The basis contains one task for each principal upset. For every antichain of Q, the disjunction of the corresponding tasks has profile exactly equal to the union of their profiles. This exactness is not implied by the individual profiles: an algorithm may satisfy different disjuncts in different executions. We establish it by constructing, for every algorithm in each maximal class outside the target union, a single admissible fair execution violating all selected predicates simultaneously. Consequently, the realizable profiles form the entire finite distributive lattice Up(Q): there are exactly 54 profiles, counted by the antichain polynomial 1 + 13z + 24z^2 + 16z^3, and each has a canonical disjunctive representation using at most three principal tasks.
  We also identify six tasks whose solvability signatures recover every inclusion and incomparability in Q, and prove that six is minimum even among arbitrary separating tasks. Their profiles are precisely the principal upsets generated by the join-irreducible elements of Q. In contrast, any task family generating every profile by exact disjunctions must contain all thirteen principal profiles. Thus our exact disjunctive basis has minimum size and is unique at the profile level.

title: A Decade in a Day: Synthesizing Agent-Native Interfaces from Human-Oriented Software Evolution
summary: Large language model agents are emerging as an important new class of users of desktop applications. However, existing desktop interfaces were designed for human end users or application developers, leaving agents to interpret visual controls or discover and compose low-level software operations. This mismatch can hinder even capable agents, yet it remains unclear what interface properties make desktop software easier for agents to use. To study this question, we treat software evolution as a natural source of interface variation and introduce DeskIF-Bench, a benchmark of 255 artifact-verified tasks across six desktop applications. By holding the task, agent, and verifier fixed while varying the software release, we measure how interface changes affect agent performance. Across two models and six applications, the newest release consistently outperforms the oldest. Trajectory analysis identifies three relevant interface properties: discoverability, granularity, and observability. Guided by these properties, we develop ANIS, a framework that synthesizes agent-native interfaces from the capabilities of installed applications. On an expanded evaluation of 368 tasks across eight applications, atomic interfaces improve success over native SDK use by 3.8 and 3.5 percentage points with DeepSeek V4 Flash and Claude Haiku 4.5, respectively, while reducing online token usage by approximately 73%. Goal-level commands further raise success to 74.5% and 67.4%, respectively.

title: Ghostline: a six-node Wi-Fi CSI motion tracker with node-to-node Links. System description and a pilot evaluation
comment: 18 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables. Data and analysis scripts archived at doi:10.5281/zenodo.23337813
summary: Ghostline is a device-free motion tracking system built on six ESP32-S3 Wi-Fi boards and one consumer router. The boards' Wi-Fi driver reports channel state information (CSI) for every received frame with the sender's address, and a modified open-source firmware forwards both, so every board carries a CSI stream for the router and for each other board: seven radios give up to 36 directed Links over 21 Spans instead of a star of six. Each Link is compared with a self-forming quiet Baseline, disturbed Links vote on a floor grid, and the grid becomes anonymous Tracks. The system was built and run during a three-day hackathon in an ordinary room. We describe it in full and report a pilot evaluation with one walker: spoken cues at seven marked positions, a two-minute free walk and five minutes of empty room, synchronised to video within 0.18 s (median). Walking between marks, the Track lay a median 0.85 m from the straight path and 1.56 m (95% CI 1.29 to 2.83) from a cue-based reference trajectory (constant speed between cues, not measured positions), with 46% of walk updates within 2 m of it; the free walk was tracked in 94% of updates. The limits: a standing person is lost within seconds, a false Track appeared in 15.9% and 2.9% of updates in two empty-room periods, and informal runs that afternoon did not separate two walkers. Two offline replays through the same pipeline show where this comes from: with the node-to-node Links removed and settings unchanged, the tracked share of walk updates falls from 90% to 19% and the free walk from 96% to 60%; a plain radio tomographic image on the same per-Span evidence, at the same false rate, matches the grid and tracker at 2 m (48% against 47%) and is ahead at 1 m (36% against 21%). On this recording the Tracks depend on the Link set, and the imaging stage adds no measurable accuracy. We state what the pilot establishes and what it does not.

title: Quota-Based Aging for Prediction-Guided Scheduling in LLM Serving
comment: 8 pages, 10 figures. Accepted for publication at the 45th IEEE International Performance, Computing, and Communications Conference (IPCCC 2026), Austin, TX, November 2026
summary: Large language model (LLM) serving systems use token-level continuous batching to improve resource utilization, but heterogeneous response lengths complicate request scheduling. Prediction-guided short-first scheduling reduces average latency but can severely delay long requests, while unrestricted aging may over-promote delayed long requests under congestion. We propose Quota-Based Aging (QBA), a lightweight policy that combines predicted short-first admission with quota-bounded, debt-enforced promotion of aged predicted-long requests. We also use a reduced M/G/n queueing surrogate, calibrated from simulator traces, to explain first-order mean-latency trends. QBA is evaluated using a serving-aware event-driven simulator that models decode-priority batching, chunked prefill, token-budget constraints, and KV-cache-safe admission. We compare QBA with FCFS, predicted short-first, and aggressive aging under asymmetric prediction errors on synthetic and production-derived workloads. The evaluation considers queueing delay, throughput, utilization, and class-conditional tail performance. Results show that QBA provides a controllable middle ground between aggressive short-first prioritization and unrestricted aging, substantially reducing long-request tail latency while retaining much of the mean-latency benefit of prediction-guided scheduling.

title: Grounding Deep Learning Framework Testing in Data Flow
comment: 22 pages, 6 figures, 7 tables
summary: Data flow underlies deep learning (DL) framework execution, including automatic differentiation and operator-fusion optimization. Bugs involving data flow can cause incorrect results or unexpected behavior. Existing testing methods represent models primarily by operator topology, omitting runtime tensor values and properties and operator input requirements. They therefore cannot distinguish data flows in models with similar topologies, even when these differences affect framework behavior. We introduce the Tensor Flow Graph (TFG) to capture runtime tensor states and operator input requirements. Its nodes represent operators and their input requirements, while its edges record tensor values and properties. Building on the TFG, we propose FlowMuT, a mutation-based testing method grounded in data flow. Mutations are represented as constrained subgraph replacements, with mutation operators derived from prior work and an analysis of mutable data flow objects. In each round, FlowMuT builds a TFG for the seed model, pairs mutation operators with TFG sites, and filters illegal candidates using data flow constraints. It uses LinUCB to select a candidate based on coverage and impact, executes the mutant, updates selection feedback, and uses each accepted mutant as the next seed. We evaluate FlowMuT on PyTorch and MindSpore using representative models from diverse application scenarios. FlowMuT submitted 55 bug reports for cases missed by all baseline methods; developers confirmed 41 reports and fixed the bugs described in 7 reports. FlowMuT achieves 43.4% higher data flow diversity than the strongest baseline and a legal mutant rate of 96.7%, compared with 86.4% without constraints. These results show that testing from a data flow perspective is practical and effective.

title: Learning to Sync at the Edge: Client-Side Adaptive Synchronization for Federated Learning
comment: 9 pages, 8 figures, 8 tables. Accepted to IEEE SEC 2026
summary: The scalability and performance of edge federated learning are fundamentally constrained by synchronization bottlenecks. Clients operate under heterogeneous compute, time-varying communication conditions, and, in some settings, privacy constraints, yet synchronization is often still handled with fixed schedules. However, synchronization decisions are often made outside the client, even though the client directly observes local progress, resource state, and communication conditions. We present a client-side reinforcement learning synchronization framework in which each client decides during training whether to upload, download, synchronize bidirectionally, or defer communication. The framework places a lightweight scheduler alongside the local model and formulates synchronization as a resource-aware control problem driven by local learning and system state. We study this framework on two representative edge workloads, spatiotemporal traffic forecasting and image classification. Across both settings, adaptive client-side synchronization improves the accuracy-cost trade-off, reducing system cost in traffic forecasting while maintaining competitive cost and improving final accuracy in image classification. We also consider privacy-constrained settings, where synchronization must account for not only latency and energy but also privacy expenditure. Overall, our results show that synchronization in edge federated learning is better treated as an adaptive client-side control problem than only as a server-side coordination mechanism.

title: A Distributed View from a Single GPU: RankLens for Distributed Training
comment: 12pages, 9 figures
summary:
Modern distributed training is costly to debug, tune, and analyze because faithful analysis often requires repeated target-scale executions. We observe that many analysis tasks depend on the original distributed execution path, but not on full all-rank execution. We present RankLens, a single-rank emulation system that runs one survivor rank on a single GPU while preserving the target job's distributed semantics. The survivor rank executes the original training program and performs real local computation. At communication boundaries, the system replaces real multi-rank communication with task-dependent semantics, selectively restoring recorded communication results and recorded or estimated completion timing while preserving the asynchronous dependencies required for analysis. This enables replay from real executions and supports analysis, debugging, and tuning with existing debuggers and performance analysis tools.
  We evaluate the system on DeepSpeed and Megatron-LM across 8-64-GPU target configurations. RankLens achieves 100% training-tensor communication-structure match, keeps emulation timing error below 5%, supports local anomaly reproduction and execution analysis, and reduces the resource requirement of these analyses from target-scale clusters to a single GPU.

title: BRQGen: Towards Adaptive Completeness Assessment and Follow-Up Question Generation for Bug Reports
summary: Many bug reports lack the necessary information required to reproduce issues. In early studies, large language models have been employed to generate follow-up questions to enhance incomplete reports. However, they ask a fixed number of questions regardless of whether the report is incomplete. We propose BRQGen, an iterative framework that identifies missing or ambiguous information in bug reports and generates targeted follow-up questions, only if necessary. Reports with no identified gaps are classified as sufficient. When the author responds, BRQGen evaluates whether the answers provide the requested information and generates further questions for any exposed gaps. We curated a novel dataset of 429 incomplete bug reports from Home Assistant and Brave Browser, each containing at least one maintainer follow-up question. Each question is mapped to the author's answer and assigned a label indicating whether the requested information could have been provided directly through the issue template. Earlier maintainer requests were associated with author responses, whereas delayed requests were associated with no response. Among responding authors, requests within one hour received median replies after 0.52 hours in Home Assistant and 1.45 hours in Brave, versus 9.76 and 13.49 hours after four hours. BRQGen covered 35.4% (Qwen 3.8 Flash) to 51.8% (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash) of the 1,073 ground-truth follow-up questions. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash managed to ask 45.7% of all detailed questions and 63.9% of all generic questions. Gemini 3 Flash Preview reached the highest macro-F1 for completeness assessment of 49.3%, but with a post-hoc analysis by getting only the gaps with high severities, Qwen 3.8 Flash reaches 73.6% macro-F1 score. Completeness assessment improved when at least one identified gap had high severity, and nearly all ground-truth questions were captured within the first two iterations.

title: TurboProm: Low Cost and High Performance Metrics Observability at Scale
summary:
Many large enterprise and cloud deployments rely on metrics observability solutions (e.g., Prometheus) to monitor key performance indicators of system health (e.g., CPU, memory, network, app-level statistics). Monitoring and analyzing these metrics presents a significant challenge in terms of cost-latency tradeoffs at scale. Ideally, system operators would like immediately deployable and backwards compatible solutions to improve the cost-latency tradeoffs without significant impact on the fidelity of their observability applications. Unfortunately, existing solutions including state-of-art timeseries databases and custom approximate querying solutions fail on one or more aspects.
  In this paper, we present the design and implementation of TurboProm, a backwards-compatible drop-in accelerator for metrics observability deployments. TurboProm recasts metrics analytics tasks using a semantic-preserving summary view rather than classical query-centric view. Instead of estimating query results on raw timeseries metrics data, TurboProm uses semantic-preserving summaries that enable high-fidelity analytics with significant cost-latency improvements. We present a practical implementation of TurboProm that can be retrofitted to any existing observability deployment. We evaluate TurboProm on diverse real and synthetic workloads against state-of-art solutions and show that it can provide significant reduction in query latency and cost. TurboProm is open-source at https://github.com/ProjectASAP/ASAPQuery.

title: LunaTP: Enabling Efficient and Scalable Tensor Product for Equivariant MLIPs
comment: 26 pages, 11 figures
summary: Equivariant machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) promise atomistic simulations with accuracy approaching that of quantum-mechanical calculations. However, the high computational cost of their core Clebsch--Gordan tensor product (CGTP) convolutions severely limits model scalability and efficiency. In this paper, we rethink the parallel execution of CGTP convolutions and introduce LunaTP. Built on node-centric execution, LunaTP exploits path-group parallelism and multi-level reuse to accelerate CGTP convolutions and higher-order derivative computation while preserving the underlying mathematical formulation. On an NVIDIA H100 GPU, LunaTP achieves kernel speedups of up to 250.0$\times$ over e3nn and 17.1$\times$ over OpenEquivariance. It also delivers end-to-end training throughput gains of up to 28.7$\times$ over e3nn and 3.11$\times$ over OpenEquivariance. Finally, LunaTP demonstrates scalability and robust performance across models, workload scales, and GPUs, delivering substantial acceleration for training and atomistic simulation with high-accuracy equivariant MLIPs.

title: When Agent Evaluation Becomes Unreliable: An Empirical Study of Oracle Failures and Configuration-Dependent Measurement in an LLM Agent Benchmark
comment: Submitted to Empirical Software Engineering
summary:
Agent evaluation harnesses are software systems that run test suites, generate inputs, and decide outcomes with test oracles. This paper audits such software for reliability defects that score tables cannot reveal.
  We introduce an oracle-integrity auditing approach with five state-integrity invariants and three known-answer controls. We evaluate it by injecting seven oracle defect classes across two task domains and a synthetic domain. All injected defect classes are detected, and the repaired oracle has no false positives. Applied to an agent benchmark, the audit reveals a reward-function defect that changes the environment state before post-run scoring. Across 4,320 episodes, replay-based correction changes database-pass labels from 4,194 to 2,883 and reduces measured success from 94.3% to 65.5%.
  We also study configuration-dependent measurement effects. A component ablation over 3,240 episodes shows that the agent's policy documents, tool descriptions, and tool error strings influence observed trajectory reliability, with tool descriptions showing the largest exploratory effect (-9.2 pp) and error strings the smallest (-5.3 pp). A second task domain reverses the sign of the language effect, so the result is bounded to the tested configuration.
  Finally, we report a portability boundary: the auditing approach cannot validate a second independently implemented benchmark because the required reference terminal state cannot be reconstructed from its recorded API-call log.
  The paper releases a replication package containing the auditing suite, fault-injection catalogue, frozen records, deviation logs, and offline analysis entry points without network access, API keys, or model calls.

title: DualColl: Throughput-Optimal Bandwidth-Bound Collective Communications via Fractional Tree Packing
comment: 20 pages, 3 figures
summary:
Large-scale distributed training increasingly makes collective communication bandwidth-bound. In modern GPU clusters, communication libraries such as NCCL implement collectives including AllReduce over heterogeneous interconnects such as NVLink, InfiniBand, and Ethernet, making efficient use of available network bandwidth a central systems challenge.
  ForestColl showed that collective communication on such fabrics can be formulated using fractional tree packing; its scalable polynomial-time construction is developed for AllGather, with AllReduce obtained by composing AllGather and ReduceScatter. We present DualColl, which targets bandwidth-bound AllReduce directly. Under the tree-based AllReduce model, DualColl applies a Garg--Könemann-style multiplicative-weights algorithm and, for any $0<ε<1$, computes a feasible schedule whose throughput is at least $(1-ε)^2$ of the optimal AllReduce throughput. Its key component is an exact minimum-cost collective-tree oracle that projects physical-link dual prices onto a logical graph of participating ranks, reducing each iteration to shortest-path computations followed by a minimum spanning tree.
  We further extend the framework to local equal-next-hop packet-sprayed routing and to networks without explicit per-tree bandwidth control. For the latter, we introduce a tree-coupled max-min bandwidth-sharing model and show that tree duplication approximates an explicit fractional allocation with a provable accuracy-complexity tradeoff. Finally, we extend the fractional-packing framework to additional collective operations and multiple concurrent collective groups.

title: FastEEP: Fast Intra-Instance Elastic Scaling for Expert-Parallel MoE Serving
summary:
Large-scale expert parallelism (EP) has become the standard deployment configuration for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models in production. Meanwhile, the highly dynamic nature of LLM workloads requires providers to continuously adjust serving capacity to match fluctuating demand. Scaling MoE serving cannot be efficiently achieved by simply adding or removing serving instances; instead, it often requires resizing the EP group within an existing instance, which we refer to as intra-instance scaling.Existing inference engines primarily rely on instance-level scaling, which destroys and reconstructs entire serving instances, incurring substantial scaling overhead.
  We present FastEEP (Fast Elastic Expert Parallel), a fast intra-instance scaling system for MoE serving based on the principle of Partial Reuse. FastEEP reuses existing runtime state across worker execution, GPU memory, and communication by separating reusable execution structures from the resources activated by the current EP configuration. This separation enables coordinated resource reclamation and reconfiguration while preserving costly-to-reconstruct state, allowing fast EP scaling without full instance teardown and reconstruction. Our evaluation shows that FastEEP achieves 4.5x--11.7x faster scaling than the existing vLLM-based approach across different models, enabling efficient, fine-grained scaling of MoE serving.

title: Software Testing Meets Bayesian Workflow: A Literature-Driven Artifact Study of Probabilistic Programs
summary: Automated testing is an effective software quality assurance method, but it is rarely used for probabilistic models. This is despite the heavy use of probabilistic programming for data analytics in research and engineering, where the consequences of errors are dire. A key obstacle is the specification of testable correctness properties for probabilistic models, known as the oracle problem. Like machine learning, probabilistic programming is used precisely where no analytical specification exists: had we been able to write one, we would have written an algorithm instead of fitting a model. An alternative is partial, proxy correctness specifications. The statistics literature already offers many, but as quality guidelines that require human judgment: comparing plots, visually analyzing shapes of distributions, assessing whether parameter values are ''far'' or ''close enough''. These guidelines are not systematically automated. In this work, we elicit, implement, and study testable correctness properties of probabilistic models.
