We extract 17 broadly applicable properties for probabilistic models from one of the most widely used textbooks in Bayesian data analysis, Statistical Rethinking by McElreath. For each property, we select and implement a test oracle, and study its utility for automatic testing, using a population of 59 probabilistic models from academic and industrial sources. We find realistic use cases (models under test) for all the properties. We observe that the vast majority of tests are not flaky in practice, despite the theoretical potential for flakiness. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to investigate the effectiveness of mutation testing for probabilistic models, showing that standard mutation operators do not capture faults tracked by the probabilistic properties.

title: MODAIC: Coordinated Asynchrony for Decentralized Multimodal Learning
summary: Multimodal decentralized learning enables collaboration across heterogeneous edge devices without sharing raw data, but differing modality sets create coupled computation and communication bottlenecks. Multimodal agents support cross-modal alignment while training more model components and sharing bandwidth across multiple modality overlays. Under bandwidth limits, these agents can become hot spots: transfers miss aggregation windows, and their updates become stale or underrepresented, degrading worst-agent accuracy. Asynchrony removes global blocking but does not by itself coordinate local cross-modal interaction with timely peer-update exchange. We present MODAIC (Modality-Decoupled Asynchrony with Interleaved Coordination), a wait-free system that coordinates local modality progress, peer-to-peer update delivery, and aggregation under heterogeneous compute and bandwidth. Hierarchical asynchrony lets modalities progress independently while enforcing reciprocal feature exchange; load-aware update fetching overlaps training with communication, limits concurrent serving load, and reuses late arrivals; and consensus-aware peer selection uses lightweight metadata to account for update availability, peer participation, and loss similarity without active probing. We implement MODAIC as a containerized multi-agent framework and evaluate it on local and cross-region cloud testbeds. Across AVE and KU-HAR, MODAIC improves average accuracy and multimodal worst-agent performance. On AVE at 200 Mbps per agent, it improves multimodal worst-agent accuracy by 11.0 percentage points at 1000 seconds over the strongest baseline. On the cloud testbed, it reduces time-to-accuracy by up to 30%. Ablations show that simpler load-balancing and delayed-aggregation variants leave a worst-agent accuracy gap, and stress tests show tolerance to WAN variability and partial tracker unavailability.

title: Tremulant: Latency in Serverless Platforms beyond the 99th Percentile
summary:
Function-as-a-Service (FaaS) increases developer productivity by removing operational concerns such as managing hardware and software runtimes. Because function instances are started on demand, some requests must wait for a new instance, called a cold start. These are a common obstacle to more widespread adoption of FaaS, as they lead to unpredictable latency spikes that are not acceptable for some use cases. To solve this, many cold start optimizations have been implemented.
  However, comparatively little attention has been directed towards the slowest warm starts. With improvements in cold start times, slow warm starts emerge as a new problem for extreme tail events. By analyzing a dataset of several million requests across seven FaaS platforms, we show that the long tail of slow warm starts can be hundreds of times slower than their median performance, while a virtual machine we use as a baseline is substantially more consistent. We confirm this across four independent public datasets spanning 2020 to 2025, so the effect is neither new nor specific to one platform. Moreover, the warm share among the slowest calls starts to rise again at the highest percentiles: the most extreme latencies are not only cold starts, and cold-start mitigation alone cannot remove them.

title: Domain-Knowledge Driven Configuration Tuning of Kubernetes Workloads
summary: Industrial software applications often require engineers to tune the software deployment platform. Configuration tuning identifies valuable configurations that minimize costs while ensuring the application performance. However, finding these configurations is difficult. The number of tunable configuration parameters in industrial applications is large, and engineers cannot assess different configurations in production because users may experience performance degradation. This work targets Kubernetes: A system for automating the deployment, scaling, and management of containerized applications. This paper proposes a domain-knowledge-driven solution for finding configurations of industrial applications in a practical time. The solution relies on a catalog of constraints encountered by domain experts in similar applications. Depending on the problem under analysis, engineers can customize the optimization problem by selecting the relevant constraints from the catalog for the application at hand. We rely on two alternative solvers to find an optimal configuration: The first is based on heuristics, while the second reuses existing optimization-based solutions. We implemented our solution within an industrial tool from a software company specializing in performance engineering and optimization. We compare our solution to a baseline, considering a set of predefined configuration values provided by engineers. Our results confirm the effectiveness of our solution: Compared to the baseline, the heuristic-based and optimization-based solutions provide significant average savings of 11591 USD/mo and 15874 USD/mo per Kubernetes, respectively, accounting for 24.03% and 32.90% of the costs, in practical time (0.71 seconds per extraction for the heuristic-based and 45.54 seconds per extraction for the optimization-based solution).

title: Revisiting Cauchy-Schwarz Norm Bounds for SDC Detection in LLM Inference
summary:
Large Language Models (LLMs) execute billions of floating-point operations per output token across many hardware accelerators. At this scale, hardware-induced faults can bypass system-level detection mechanisms and cause Silent Data Corruption (SDC). Algorithm-Based Fault Tolerance (ABFT) is the state-of-the-art technique for protecting matrix multiplication from such faults, but it incurs non-negligible computational overhead and requires thresholds to distinguish hardware-induced errors from floating-point roundoff. In this paper, we revisit Cauchy--Schwarz Norm Bounds (CSNB) as a low-overhead alternative for detecting SDC during LLM inference. We compare CSNB against ABFT through controlled fault injection and evaluate the runtime overhead of both verification and threshold determination across multiple model sizes, batch sizes, and generation lengths.
  Our results show that, on average, CSNB retains 99% of the fault detection capability of ABFT for the evaluated dense linear layers while reducing verification overhead by 87% and threshold determination overhead by 67%. For Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) router gate computations, however, CSNB retains only 55% of the fault detection capability of ABFT. These findings suggest that CSNB is a promising low-overhead alternative for protecting dense linear layers in LLM inference, while checksum-based verification remains preferable for the evaluated MoE router gate.

title: DeepGroundRepair: From API-Grounded Generation to Shape-Aware Repair for Deep Learning Programs
summary:
Deep learning programs are fundamental to modern AI applications, and automatically generating them from natural language requirements can substantially reduce DL development effort. Large language models have demonstrated promising capabilities for this direction. However, generated DL programs often remain unreliable because they must satisfy domain specific API usage constraints and tensor shape dependencies, violations of which can cause API level syntactic issues and runtime failures. Existing retrieval augmented generation and feedback guided code repair methods do not adequately address these DL specific constraints.
  In this paper, we propose DeepGroundRepair, a three stage framework that establishes a generation localization repair workflow to improve the reliability of LLM-generated DL programs. Its key idea is to progressively narrow the generation and repair spaces using DL specific knowledge and runtime tensor information. Specifically, it grounds generation in task-relevant API knowledge, localizes the upstream causes of tensor shape mismatch failures, and uses runtime tensor shapes to guide parameter repair.
  We evaluate DeepGroundRepair on the 100 model-level DL programming tasks in DeepEval using six open-weight LLMs across TensorFlow, PyTorch, and PaddlePaddle. We compare it with four baselines: two generation-only methods and their counterparts incorporating traceback guided self debugging. The results show that, relative to these baselines, DeepGroundRepair reduces the combined number of API-level syntactic issues by an average of 5.4 per 10 program files and achieves an average relative improvement of 85.3% in code executability. Compared with the two self debugging baselines, it improves semantic consistency by an average of 18.1% and reduces token cost by an average of 28.4%.

title: Orrery: Modeling and Simulation of GPU-direct MPI Communication with SimGrid
comment: Accepted as a short paper at the PMBS 2026 workshop (held in conjunction with SC26)
summary: Simulation of HPC applications is an essential tool for analyzing system design trade-offs and enabling effective hardware--software co-design. As modern supercomputers increasingly rely on GPU acceleration, MPI implementations have evolved to support GPU-aware communication, enabling direct GPU data transfers. Modeling these mechanisms is therefore critical for simulating HPC applications on current systems. In this paper, we introduce Orrery, an interposition layer built on SimGrid's SMPI to model GPU-aware MPI communication using existing collective implementations and flow-based simulation. Orrery intercepts GPU memory allocations, kernel launches, data transfers, and MPI operations, and models their execution in SimGrid according to target system specifications, enabling simulation without requiring physical GPUs. We validate Orrery using CUDA-aware MPI microbenchmarks and a Jacobi solver on up to 32 nodes of the MUSICA supercomputer and demonstrate that it reproduces key GPU-aware MPI mechanisms.

title: AIPOCH Open-Science: An Open-Source AI Research Workbench with Reproducible .science Packages
comment: 23 pages; 2 main figures, 3 tables, a graphical abstract and Supplementary Figure S1
summary: AI-assisted research leaves instructions, computations, artifact revisions and checks whose relationships matter when another researcher receives the work. We present AIPOCH Open-Science, an open-source research workbench with portable .science session packages, and specify an exchange contract for these recorded relationships. Version and assessment targets remain attributable while receiving-workspace identifiers can be remapped, eligible contents can be omitted explicitly, and imported history remains separate from a writable fork. A controlled session tested an incorrect first version, a reviewed correction, an unreviewed revision and a planned but unexecuted step. We compared complete and partial exports with source records extracted independently of the exporter, then inspected imports into separate projects within the same installation. Both conditions retained the tested version and review associations, kept the unreviewed revision distinct from earlier assessments and represented excluded content as unavailable. A documentation-rich ordinary directory also supplied evidence for all seven static inspection questions. A separate registry case connected a table to its recorded task, execution and review; offline execution of its retained script and fixed input reproduced two saved CSV tables byte for byte. The study contributes an implemented exchange contract and a controlled examination of its preservation rules, content-selection constraints and interpretation boundaries.

title: A Distributed Energy Relay Framework for Sustainable Drone Missions
summary: Limited battery endurance remains a major obstacle to persistent UAV missions. Existing energy-replenishment approaches typically rely on battery-swapping/charging infrastructure or on ground vehicles with accessible road networks - assumptions that may not hold in infrastructure-less regions (ILRs) such as remote wilderness, mountainous terrain, and disaster-stricken areas. We formulate energy resupply in ILRs as a distinct logistics problem, in which energy itself must be projected into a region with no pre-existing infrastructure, and proposes a Distributed Energy Relay Framework that enables cooperative energy delivery using porter drones. The framework introduces a Transportation-by-Relay-and-Cache (TRC) mechanism, in which drones relay battery resources toward a mission location. Additional models are developed to characterize battery transportation capacity, relay amplification, energy-delivery capability, operational cost, and reliability. Based on these models, stations independently evaluate their delivery capability and submit bids to a mission coordinator, which selects an energy-delivery coalition that satisfies mission requirements while minimizing cost. Analytical evaluation illustrates the impact of battery characteristics and drone capabilities on energy projection and demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed framework for sustaining UAV missions in ILRs.

title: Deleting Code Without Losing Knowledge: Regenerative Software for Python Libraries
comment: 53 pages
summary: In the age of "Software 3.0", when a complete program can be rewritten in minutes by an agent, the traditional approach of relying on code as the sole source of truth becomes questionable. Fowler advocated for a set of seven primitives, which lay the framework for regenerative software, so that programs can be deleted and rebuilt without losing their knowledge. The knowledge lives in machine-readable records in a tracked directory, from which a *regeneration bundle* is built for each unit. The regeneration bundle is a single file with the module's architecture, intent, decisions, public contract, evaluations, and consumers, but no implementation, plus the one dependency module it may import. The open-source package spotregen implements these primitives and provides a graphical user interface. This report presents a first application of Fowler's primitives to the safety-critical forecasting library spotforecast2-safe. During the first experiments, the Claude Code session that orchestrated the study consumed more than 43 million tokens, almost all of them its own history re-sent with every request. This motivated the switch to an architecture that is built on local models. Deterministic checks and the maintainer judged the results. The report contains executable examples for every primitive. Each example runs spotregen against the repository or against a throw-away copy of it.

title: Semantic Edge-Cloud Communication for Real-Time Urban Traffic Digital Twins
comment: 6 pages, 4 figures, accepted to IEEE Global Communications (Globecom) Conference, 2026
summary: Urban traffic systems are becoming increasingly complex, demanding real-time traffic perception, proactive collision prediction, and intelligent management to improve safety and reduce congestion. Although AI-driven traffic management has shown strong promise, its success relies on diverse, high-quality data spanning critical scenarios such as collisions, near-collisions, and traffic rule violations. Digital twins offer a powerful solution by enabling synchronized virtual replicas of physical traffic environments for real-time monitoring, collision prediction, traffic-flow optimization, and diverse realistic scenario generation. However, continuously synchronizing a high-fidelity urban traffic digital twin through edge surveillance cameras requires substantial edge-cloud communication, and transmitting raw video streams leads to severe bandwidth and latency constraints. To overcome this challenge, this paper proposes a semantic communication-based edge-cloud framework for real-time urban traffic digital twin applications. By leveraging edge intelligence to extract and transmit only task-relevant semantic traffic information instead of full video feeds, the proposed framework significantly reduces communication overhead while preserving the essential dynamics needed for accurate real-time digital twin reconstruction. Experimental results demonstrate more than 99% transmission savings and an average trajectory reconstruction error of only 0.12 m, confirming the proposed framework as an effective, scalable, and low-latency solution for AI-enabled urban traffic digital twin applications.

title: VulnBump: A Benchmark for Fixing Vulnerable Dependencies in Real Projects While Keeping the Build and Tests Green
comment: 22 pages, 5 figures. Code and data: https://github.com/snyk-labs/snyk-vulnbump
summary: Software composition analysis (SCA) tools report far more vulnerable dependencies than teams fix: in Snyk Open Source production data, 94% of vulnerability findings have a known fixed version, yet only about 10% are resolved. Agentic coding tools could close this gap, but no benchmark evaluates them on vulnerability-driven upgrades in real, runnable projects across ecosystems, verified independently of the agent. We present VulnBump: 307 upgrade tasks covering 2,066 fixable vulnerabilities in 43 repositories across six package managers, matched to Snyk Open Source production vulnerability distributions. An upgrade passes only if, in a fresh container, dependencies resolve, a rescan shows the targeted vulnerabilities fixed, the project builds, and every previously passing test still passes. A non-agentic baseline that only applies Snyk's recommended version passes 46.9% of upgrades; with the same model (Claude Sonnet 5.5), Snyk's Evo Remediation Agent passes 90.2%, Claude Code + Snyk scan 77.5% and Claude Code unaided 59.6%. The agents fail in opposite ways: Claude Code mostly leaves the vulnerability in place, whereas most of Evo Remediation Agent's failures break the build or tests. An SCA scanner is a key tool for agents: Snyk's guidance raises Claude Code's PASS rate by 17.9 percentage points; without it, Claude Code often settles on a still-vulnerable version. Yet knowing the target is not enough: given the same Snyk findings, Evo Remediation Agent's purpose-built harness passes 12.7 points more than Claude Code + Snyk scan. Major framework migrations remain hard for all harnesses. Because the agents keep projects working at similar rates, evaluating remediation quality in dependency upgrades requires verifying the fix, the build and the tests together.

title: TurboProm: Low Cost and High Performance Metrics Observability at Scale
summary:
Many large enterprise and cloud deployments rely on metrics observability solutions (e.g., Prometheus) to monitor key performance indicators of system health (e.g., CPU, memory, network, app-level statistics). Monitoring and analyzing these metrics presents a significant challenge in terms of cost-latency tradeoffs at scale. TurboProm recasts metrics analytics tasks using a semantic-preserving summary view rather than classical query-centric view. We present a practical implementation of TurboProm that can be retrofitted to any existing observability deployment. We evaluate TurboProm on diverse real and synthetic workloads against state-of-art solutions and show that it can provide significant reduction in query latency and cost. TurboProm is open-source at https://github.com/ProjectASAP/ASAPQuery.

title: Why Agentic Workflows Fail: A Taxonomy Derived from Literature and Empirical Data
summary: Agentic workflows combine large language models with planning, memory, tools, execution environments, and iterative feedback. Their failures are difficult to diagnose because the same user-visible symptom may originate from model behavior, workflow orchestration, external tools, infrastructure, or their interaction. This paper presents a source-aware taxonomy of agentic workflow failures and applies it to evidence from academic literature and GitHub. The taxonomy combines source attribution with three empirical dimensions: a concrete failure-type dictionary, workflow-stage localization, and agent-capability localization. Its central structure is a two-axis localization matrix: workflow stages form the horizontal process axis and agent capabilities form the vertical functional axis. This design moves beyond taxonomies that mainly classify final failure manifestations by localizing intermediate process states inside agent operation. Our empirical comparison shows that literature-derived failures emphasize planning, reasoning, learning, perception, and knowledge-related mechanisms, whereas GitHub-derived failures concentrate on execution-stage, actuation-related, tool, API, and infrastructure failures. The dominant hotspot is iterative execution and actuation. These findings indicate that agentic workflow reliability should be treated as a systems problem rather than only a model-output problem. The taxonomy provides a basis for structured evaluation, root cause analysis, failure injection, and engineering triage.

title: Energy-Aware Agentic Orchestration for Multi-Site Service Deployment
comment: Accepted author manuscript for publication in the Proceedings of the 2026 IEEE Future Networks World Forum (FNWF 2026), Lisbon, Portugal, October 26-28, 2026
summary: Energy-aware orchestration across geographically distributed infrastructures is increasingly important as data centers absorb growing Artificial Intelligence (AI) workloads. However, existing approaches often exclude the energy cost of automated decision-making from system-level sustainability assessments. This paper presents an energy-aware agentic orchestration framework that treats Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning as a measurable component of the control loop. We compare single-shot tool calling, ReAct, and plan-and-execute strategies on a multi-site Kubernetes testbed spanning two European data centers and instrumented at layers ranging from power distribution units to per-pod energy attribution. Using ten natural-language orchestration intents with varying decision complexity, we show that reasoning strategy and intent complexity strongly influence graphics processing unit (GPU) energy consumption during orchestration decisions. ReAct and plan-and-execute generated executable tool calls across all evaluated intents but required multiple LLM inferences, whereas the single-shot configuration was less costly but non-actionable. Prefix caching reduced mean ReAct GPU energy consumption by 29.4%. For the evaluated lightweight workload, the infrastructure-energy changes observed within the one-second measurement window were insufficient to offset the measured GPU decision energy. These findings demonstrate the importance of accounting for reasoning overhead when assessing the sustainability of AI-native orchestration and motivate energy-budgeted selection of agent strategies.

title: Cross-Project Bug Localization: What Works, What Doesn't, and Why
comment: 25 pages, 11 tables, 8 figures
summary: Bug localization models require substantial within-project training data that newly active or small open-source projects rarely have. Cross-project learning (CPL) promises to close this gap by reusing labeled bugs from mature projects, but prior CPL studies evaluate a single model against ample-data within-project baselines that data-scarce projects cannot reach. We ask whether CPL's effectiveness is a property of the transfer setting or depends on model architecture. We evaluate three architecturally distinct models, embedding-based BLAZE, convolutional TRANP-CNN, and GNN-based adversarial COOBA, on 63 source to target pairs from 13 open-source Python projects under identical bug corpora, data splits, retrieval candidates, and baselines. The primary baseline is within-project limited training (WP-small, 20% of target labels, the same target-side share as CP-transfer). CPL outperforms WP-small most clearly for TRANP-CNN (Cohen's d = 0.95, win rate 81.0%, p < 0.001, robust to clustering pairs by target project), and less so for BLAZE (d = 0.49, win rate 60.3%, p = 0.002; not significant once pairs are clustered by target). COOBA, under our re-implementation, shows a small gain that does not survive multiple-comparison correction (d = 0.27, p = 0.027). Negative transfer affects 9.5% of TRANP-CNN pairs and 30.2% of BLAZE's and COOBA's. Cross-model direction agreement is only 44-54%: the same pair can help one architecture and harm another, although the models' gains are positively correlated (rho = 0.24-0.42). CPL outcomes are therefore architecture-dependent: practitioners should validate CPL for their chosen model, and CPL studies should report results per architecture.

title: Conflict-Aware Autonomous Resource Orchestration for 5G Edge Slicing Using Multi-Agent Systems and LLMs
comment: Accepted author manuscript for publication in the Proceedings of the 2027 IEEE Consumer Communications & Networking Conference (CCNC 2027), Las Vegas, Nevada, USA, January 9-12, 2027
summary: 5G edge network slicing must reconcile two coupled requirements: understanding high-level operator intent and reallocating scarce computing and bandwidth resources under dynamic contention. Centralized optimization can face computational and responsiveness challenges under rapidly changing edge contention, and Multi-Agent System (MAS)-based auctions can support resource arbitration but still depend on operator-defined economic parameters and priorities. Embedding a Large Language Model (LLM) directly in a recurring control loop, by contrast, may introduce non-negligible inference latency and non-deterministic behavior. This paper proposes a two-timescale architecture that addresses this gap: an LLM-based Strategist translates natural-language network intents into economic policy parameters (budget, income, and bidding-aggressiveness) at the macro scale, while a deterministic, Vickrey-inspired second-price mechanism run by SPADE-based slice agents resolves recurring resource contention at the operational scale, with the resulting allocations enforced by patching Kubernetes CPU limits and Calico CNI bandwidth annotations directly on User Plane Function pods. We evaluate the architecture end-to-end on a real Kubernetes/Open5GS edge cluster across two complementary scenarios, each repeated 30 times: a Smart-City scenario, in which natural-language public-safety intents propagate into measurable changes in slice bids and bandwidth allocations within a few auction rounds, and a Hierarchical-slicing scenario, in which the mechanism provides priority-dependent resource and QoE differentiation, adapts to abrupt demand changes, and preserves configured minimum guarantees while maintaining near-complete allocation of the shared bandwidth pool.

title: StateHarness: Maintaining Evolving Project State for Long-Horizon Coding Agents
comment: 20 pages, 4 figures, 11 tables
summary: Long-horizon coding requires agents to maintain an evolving view of the project they are changing: what problem is currently being solved, what has already been learned or modified, which other artifacts may be affected, and what work remains unresolved. When this information is scattered across a growing interaction history, local edits can become disconnected from their later consequences and progress can be difficult to carry forward. We introduce StateHarness, a runtime framework that maintains evolving project state without updating model parameters. The working agent records its current problem and hypothesis, important findings and decisions, discovered repository relationships, and unfinished work. Runtime support prompts record updates, searches for callers, tests, and documentation that may be affected by a change, and maintains a compact working brief for subsequent decisions. When behavioral signals accumulate, a separate diagnostic session revisits the recorded history and surfaces overlooked evidence. Across three repository-level evaluations, StateHarness improves task completion and several measures of change consistency. On RefactorBench, full-chain completion increases from 29.4% to 35.3% and cleanup-check accuracy from 87.0% to 95.4%. On five LHTB software-engineering tasks, mean reward improves from 0.427 to 0.576, exceeding LongHorizon-Harness at substantially lower recorded execution cost. On ChainSWE, bug-fix rate increases from 35.1% to 39.5% and residual debt decreases from 60 to 43 items, although pass-to-pass regressions increase. These results show that maintaining project state can improve long-horizon coding while introducing measurable execution and regression trade-offs.

title: Recall-Bounded Staleness for Filtered Multi-Tenant ANN Graph Indexes under Concurrent Updates
comment: 14 pages, 4 figures, 3 Pages supplemental Proof
summary: Production vector search must continuously ingest, delete, and re-tenant vectors while serving low-latency, high-recall, metadata-filtered approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) queries for many tenants with per-tenant service-level objectives. Existing graph-based ANN systems address these requirements largely in isolation, leaving recall during concurrent re-optimization without an analytical bound. We develop a graph-based index that combines streaming updates, filtered search, and multi-tenancy, with one theoretical result and two system mechanisms. Our theory decomposes per-tenant recall loss into staleness from updates not yet integrated into the graph and filtered navigability determined by the local density of points satisfying a tenant's predicate. The staleness component exhibits anti-amortization on a merge-based graph, integrating a larger batch of inserts increases recall degradation super-linearly, so larger merges do not reduce total staleness loss. Holding the insert horizon fixed while increasing merge size 20x, we observe a monotonic decrease in terminal recall@10 from 99.44% to 99.01%. For filtered search, the theory gives a parameter-free frontier-mass relationship in local predicate density and a query-averaged per-tenant recall bound. We instantiate the bound with a filter and tenant-aware staging cache and a select-not-resize scheduler with per-tenant staleness ceilings. On a FreshDiskANN substrate, the ceiling eliminates tight-tier SLA violations under the evaluated churn workload, while merge reordering changes terminal recall by only 0.02 percentage points. The results show how recall bounds can guide background maintenance without relying on merge resizing as a recall control mechanism.

title: Diff Diffusion: Predicting Edit Paths with Diffusion Models for Efficient Code Editing
comment: 15 pages, 3 figures, 6 tables. Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Diffusion Language Models: Foundations, Efficiency, and Reasoning
summary: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) are appealing for code generation because they can update many tokens in parallel, yet many are optimized for sequence synthesis rather than edit prediction. This setting is poorly matched to modern AI-assisted IDEs, where edit prediction must infer the next code change from recent edits, the current file, and cursor-local context. Such changes are usually sparse and preserve most source tokens, so regenerating a full code segment wastes computation. We propose Diff Diffusion, a diffusion-inspired LLM framework for code editing that predicts edit paths from an original snippet to its revised form. Diff Diffusion represents denoising as structured edit operations, and combines this formulation with multi-stage training and efficient parallel decoding. By focusing computation on changed regions, Diff Diffusion supports accurate low-latency edits and multi-position parallel modification. Across public edit-completion benchmarks, edit-prediction evaluations, and online validation, Diff Diffusion matches or leads autoregressive baselines while delivering 2.78 times faster inference on public edit-completion benchmarks and a 39.0% P50 model-latency reduction in production. This work provides a new modeling perspective for AI applications that require high accuracy and low latency.

title: CALIPER: Calibrating HPC/AI Network Simulators
summary: Network simulation plays an important role in HPC/AI system research by enabling exploration of network architectures, communication strategies, and system configurations at scales that may be impractical to study experimentally. Existing approaches to network simulator calibration and validation lack a principled methodology that combines parameter alignment, constrained inference, and independent validation for collective-centric HPC/AI networks. We present CALIPER, a methodology for systematic calibration and validation of HPC/AI network simulators. CALIPER distinguishes directly observable system parameters from auxiliary parameters which are configured via calibration and constrains the latter to feasible domains consistent with the target system. We evaluate CALIPER's hierarchical, scale-aware calibration and its effects on parameter identifiability and generalization using collective communication benchmarks on a reference system with up to 64-nodes at the Jülich Supercomputing Centre. Validation results show that the calibrated parameter configurations identified by CALIPER predict system performance with less than 5% mean errors across scale-up and scale-out network domains. CALIPER demonstrates that hierarchical, constrained calibration can produce simulator configurations whose predictive accuracy persists beyond the observations used for fitting.

title: State-Aware Generation of Deployable Websites from Visual Prototypes and Requirements
summary: Generating deployable websites from visual prototypes and textual requirements is increasingly feasible with multimodal models, yet keeping generated projects consistent with their prototypes remains challenging. Prototypes specify layouts and visual elements, while requirements describe interaction workflows and deployment constraints. Existing UI-to-code methods and coding agents often treat layout reconstruction, interaction implementation, and project editing separately, allowing visual elements, files, workflows, dependencies, and render evidence to lose their correspondence across generation, verification, and update. We call this problem prototype-to-project state drift. We propose VisStateCoder, a state-aware framework that maintains these correspondences in a Project State Graph. The graph connects four types of state nodes through typed links and supports prototype grounding, graph-guided generation, and render-evidence-guided scoped updates that map failed checks to affected files while preserving files outside the update scope. We evaluate VisStateCoder on Vision2Web using five foundation models across Static Webpage, Interactive Frontend, and Full-Stack Website tasks. Averaged across models, VisStateCoder improves overall scores over the strongest baseline for each model by 26.1 and 22.6 points on Interactive Frontend and Full-Stack Website tasks, respectively. It also reduces verified-state drift, measured by checks that pass in one update round but fail later, compared with alternative state representations. An annotation study of 50 tasks finds that the constructed graphs achieve 95.6% edge-level F1.

title: FORGE: Procedural Weight Generation for Sparse MoE Inference
comment: 16 pages. Accepted to ASPLOS 2027
summary: We introduce FORGE (Fast On-chip Rotor Generation for Experts), a procedural weight generation system for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) inference. Rather than storing and loading every expert weight tensor from HBM, we show how a compact accelerator inside each Streaming Multiprocessor can regenerate them on-the-fly from $O(\log^2 d)$ rotor parameters per projection. Per replaced layer, gigabytes of stored expert weights are approximated with under a megabyte of seeds. This addresses the dual memory bottleneck of autoregressive Sparse MoE decode, where per-expert FFN operations are HBM-bandwidth-bound at small routed-token counts and the aggregate expert footprint forces multi-node Expert Parallelism (EP) with all-to-all traffic. We realize the approach as the Rotor Generation Unit (RGU), a fixed-function datapath that generates FFN weight tiles without competing with Tensor Core execution. With 30% of the MoE FFN layers replaced across five Sparse MoE models, we estimate 1.3-2.8x higher system throughput at matched GPU count and 1.10-1.15x lower per-user decode latency at short context. In exchange, downstream accuracy on three model families falls below that of the same model fine-tuned without rotor replacement, and the replacement ratio controls this tradeoff. FORGE also expands KV cache capacity by 1.2-2.6x. It is agnostic to the bit width at which weights are stored, so it can compose with quantization. The RGU is fully implemented/verified in SystemVerilog at ~0.9% SM area overhead (0.032 mm^2/SM, 7nm).

title: Mobile App Analysis in the New Era: Challenges and the Road Ahead
comment: 35 pages. Minor correction: removed a sentence in Section 6.1.1 that contains an incorrect citation
summary: Mobile applications (apps) have grown into complex, multi-platform systems that support diverse services and operate within varying regulatory and distribution contexts. Traditional analysis techniques have established a strong foundation for ensuring quality, security, and compliance, but face increasing challenges as mobile apps evolve. This article presents a three-layer perspective to examine these challenges. The Artifact Layer highlights how heterogeneous code bases and protection mechanisms reduce the analyzability of packaged apps. The Runtime Layer addresses growing execution complexity, from multi-modal interactions and super-app architectures to AI-driven autonomous operations. The Ecosystem Layer considers broader contexts, including emerging platforms, fragmented distribution channels, and region-specific regulatory requirements. New characteristics across these layers interact and compound, creating difficulties that existing approaches are not designed to handle. For each layer, we identify key challenges and potential research directions, including framework-aware analysis, adaptive testing, and policy-aware compliance verification. We also discuss how large language models bring new analytical capabilities to the field, while their integration into apps raises new security and privacy concerns. This article aims to clarify where established methods fall short and highlight directions for future research in this evolving field.

title: MCCL: Measurement-based Collective Communication Library
comment: 25 pages, 17 figures, 5 tables. Accepted for publication in Proceedings of the ACM on Networking (PACMNET), Vol. 4, No. CoNEXT4, Article 55, December 2026. DOI: 10.1145/3856969
summary: Collective communication is a critical performance bottleneck in large-scale distributed training. Existing libraries and synthesis frameworks compute open-loop schedules once, assuming a static topology and peak link capacities. In production, however, persistent gray failures can silently degrade link throughput and latency for hours, causing pre-computed schedules to lose much of their efficiency during execution. In this paper, we present Measurement-based Collective Communication Library (MCCL), a collective communication library that closes the loop between runtime network measurement and dynamic schedule synthesis. MCCL passively measures GPU-to-GPU throughput, detects persistent degradation, re-synthesizes the affected communication-intensive schedules with warm-started synthesizers, and hot-swaps them without interrupting training. We validate the complete loop on a multi-node hardware prototype and use simulations to evaluate cluster-scale scenarios. In our experiments, MCCL incurs negligible overhead (<2%) while maintaining high measurement accuracy (<1.2% error) and low schedule hot-swap time (about 12 ms). Notably, under gray failures, MCCL reduces training time by up to 4.99x over static schedules on simulated training workloads for state-of-the-art LLMs such as Llama and DeepSeek.

title: SpecCloak: Probing Harmful Code Generation through Engineering Specifications
comment: 9 pages, 7 figures
summary: The code generation capabilities of large language models (LLMs) can equally be misused to implement harmful functionality, underscoring the need to understand their safety behavior in response to programming requests. While request phrasing is known to influence refusal, it remains unclear whether the form in which coding task requirements are stated affects the refusal process for malicious code generation. We introduce PseudoSpec, a template that organizes functional requirements as engineering specifications, and investigate its effects through controlled comparisons, representation analysis, and activation interventions. Across five open-weight models, removing explicit risk keywords only partially reduces refusal, whereas specification prompting substantially lowers refusal even when these keywords are retained. This reduction accompanies consistent shifts toward code-output-related representations, and interventions along condition-difference directions alter refusal behavior. Output analysis further distinguishes code-related responses from generation degeneration. Building on these findings, we propose SpecCloak, a black-box red-teaming framework combining PseudoSpec with discriminator-guided optimization, achieving an average execution-verified attack success rate of 28.91\% across eight target models on RedCode-Gen. We also introduce SpecReveal, a defense prototype combining natural-language intent reconstruction with dual-view detection without target-model fine-tuning. It achieves a 96.88\% attack detection rate in a separate prompt-detection evaluation, with false positives assessed on benign programming and specification-style inputs. These results connect specification-induced response differences to practical security consequences and identify intent reconstruction as a complementary detection approach.

title: Computing All-Pairs Shortest Communication Time Paths for Periodically Varying Satellite Networks
summary: We address the problem of designing an efficient algorithm for computing the all-pairs shortest-time paths in time-varying networks, specifically targeting the dynamic topological characteristics of low earth orbit (LEO) satellite constellations. We model such temporal graphs as $G = (V, E_t)$, where $V=\{1, 2,\ldots , n\}$ is the set of $n$ vertices in the graph, and $E_t$ is the set of $M$ time-varying edges considered over a total time window of size $T = Mτ$, $τ$ being the duration of each interval in that time window. For such a network, our algorithm finds the all-pair shortest paths in $O(M^2n^3)$-time. A key advantage of our approach is its computational structure, which mirrors two matrix multiplication steps, first in the forward direction and then in the backward direction. This structure of the algorithm makes it exceptionally suitable for parallelization on SIMD architectures like GPUs, thereby offering a significant speedup over traditional shortest-path algorithms and enabling efficient, network-wide message routing in rapidly changing LEO satellite constellations.

title: SWEPatchTest: Evaluating Software Tests Beyond Reproduction
summary: Coding agents use generated tests to decide whether a proposed patch satisfies an issue's requirements. A suite that fails on the buggy program and passes after applying the reference patch can still accept an incorrect patch or reject a correct patch. We introduce SWEPATCHTEST, a test-generation benchmark with 619 tasks from SWE-bench Pro, SWE-bench Multilingual, and DeepSWE and 82,579 candidate patches collected from coding-agent trajectories. By replaying each suite on the buggy and patched codebases, \benchmark jointly measures issue reproduction, acceptance of correct patches, and rejection of incorrect patches. Joint Validation Rate (JVR), which requires all three criteria on the same task, exposes failures hidden by single-reference evaluation: the best-performing configuration achieves only 9.21% JVR despite reproducing the reference transition on 59.29% of tasks. We further use validation scores to select and scale demonstrations for supervised fine-tuning (SFT). The resulting training recipe approximately triples JVR and improves downstream repair across three SWE-bench benchmarks. Patch discrimination thus provides both a diagnostic measure of test quality and an execution-based signal for curating agent training data.

title: Soliduzz: Finding Miscompilations in Smart-Contract Compilers with Assertion-Driven Equivalence Oracles
summary:
Smart contracts compiled to the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) can manage high-value assets and are difficult to patch after deployment. Compiler miscompilations are therefore especially dangerous: compilation succeeds, but the generated bytecode does not preserve the semantics of the source program. Existing smart-contract compiler fuzzers either focus on robustness failures or rely on differential oracles that compare compiler configurations.
  We present Soliduzz, an approach for finding miscompilations in EVM smart-contract compilers using assertion-driven equivalence oracles. Soliduzz uses product programs to encode semantic equivalence as executable assertions. The key shift is to compile these self-checking programs and let off-the-shelf fuzzers and symbolic execution engines explore the resulting bytecode for assertion violations, without requiring compiler-specific support from the analyzer.
  Soliduzz instantiates this idea with two complementary families of metamorphic transformations. The first starts from equivalent expressions and lifts them into smart-contract code that deliberately exercises EVM-specific features such as storage, data locations, control flow, contract interactions, and inline assembly. The second generalizes Equivalence Modulo Inputs (EMI) from fixed concrete inputs to symbolic input spaces. Our symbolic EMI records coverage in the original computation and uses it to guard mutations in the transformed computation. Together, these transformations produce product programs that assert that paired computations yield the same outputs.
  We evaluate Soliduzz on three EVM smart-contract compilers (solc, solx, and vyper) using several analysis tools. Overall, Soliduzz exposes 29 bugs. Of these, 24 are compiler bugs: 6 miscompilations, 17 internal compiler errors, and 1 hang. The remaining 5 are bugs in the analysis tools.

title: Assessing the Quality of Concrete Scenarios Generated from Scenario Classes for Automated Driving
summary: A scenario-based development approach has become state of the art for automated driving systems. Once a set of scenario classes covering the operational design domain is available, concrete scenarios are generated from these scenario classes, e.g., to be used for hazard analysis and risk assessment or for the system's verification and validation. For such applications, a high diversity among the generated concrete scenarios is paramount. The question arises how the quality of collections of concrete scenarios can be assessed in such a setting. In this work, we aggregate scenario distance measures into so-called quality functions that quantify the diversity of concrete scenario collections in the context of automated driving. In particular, we consider the case where scenario classes are formalized as constraint systems and the associated concrete scenario space is not explicitly known. Based on a set of desired properties we construct candidates for such quality functions and give proofs for their property fulfillment. To show the practical relevance of quality functions, we perform a variety of experiments in the context of an abstract scenario-based virtual verification toolchain for automated driving systems. More specifically, we use quality functions to compare the effectiveness of variation methods for sampling, examine the choice of different scenario distance measures, and investigate the effects of temporal aspects on concrete scenario collection quality.

title: SWE-MISBEHAVIOR: Benchmarking and Mitigating Boundary Violations in Software Coding Agents
comment: Codes and data are available at https://github.com/dxlong2000/SWE-Misbehavior
summary: We present SWE-MISBEHAVIOR, the first taxonomy and evaluation framework for diagnosing boundary-violating misbehaviors in coding agents. It contains 7.4K human-in-the-loop synthesized samples spanning three layers of agent action space: (i) Code Generation, (ii) File Management, and (iii) System Interaction. Across these categories, SWE-MISBEHAVIOR covers 11 distinct misbehaviors with a fully automated evaluation protocol, including coding-action violations, Create/Read/Update/Delete (CRUD) file misbehaviors, system integrity and abuse violations, and task-goal misalignment. Experiments on state-of-the-art open-source coding agents (e.g., OpenHands, smolagents) reveal substantial misaligned behaviors, including dependency misinterpretation (up to 98.5% of cases), unintended modification of user inputs (50.5%), and silent compromise of environment integrity (53%). Motivated by these findings, we further propose CODE-KIT, a lightweight adaptive framework that combines misbehavior-aware guidelines with novel tools to help agents avoid such failures. CODE-KIT reduces misbehaviors by 52% for smolagents and 34% for OpenHands, while simultaneously improving task completion performance.

title: DTScribe: Generating Models for Digital Twin Reporting using Local Large Language Models
summary:
The development of a digital twin brings together many stakeholders and technical components. We have previously investigated the reporting of the conceptual architecture for these digital twins as an artifact for discussion. However, we find that the activity of modeling the digital twin for visualization and consensus-building can be quite tedious and time-consuming.
  In this article, we explore the automation of model generation using large language models, targeting the model required for digital twin reporting. Our approach is designed to ingest digital twin documents and output both the conceptual architecture visualization and a reporting page for that digital twin. We first extract from the input the key details aligning with our twenty-one-characteristic Digital Twin Description Framework described in previous work. Then, we generate a description model in the Ontological Modeling Language, representing the digital twin as a constellation of models, data, enablers, and services. We utilize refinement loops with large language models acting as judges and ontological reasoning to increase artifact quality as measured by our metrics.
  We investigate how architectural and parameter choices affect artifact quality, such as how refinement loops enable local large language models to produce sufficiently high-quality results comparable to larger models. We also detail insights and lessons learned useful for practitioners, such that they can integrate our techniques to accelerate their digital twin reporting or for other model generation tasks. These insights include the use of medium-sized local models (around 20 billion parameters), the avoidance of large language models as judges and clustering for characteristic extraction, and the recommendation of at least two reasoner loops for Ontological Modeling Language refinement.

title: SolBehave: Evaluating the Behavioural Correctness of LLM-Generated Smart Contracts
summary: Large language models increasingly generate Solidity smart contracts that, once deployed, can never be patched, making a single latent fault permanent and exploitable. Yet current evaluations mostly ask only whether generated code compiles. We introduce SolBehave, a benchmark for evaluating the correctness of model-generated contracts at scale, moving beyond ad hoc unit tests. Across 250 real, reproducible Ethereum contracts, we apply three complementary tests of behavioural fidelity: differential fuzzing, historical-transaction replay, and, as our core contribution, synthetic-transaction replay guided by a Dynamic Condition Response (DCR) graph that enumerates the space of legitimate function-call sequences. Differential fuzzing compares each generated function with the original on automatically generated inputs; historical replay compares the whole contract on the transactions it actually received on-chain; DCR-guided replay compares it on sequences of calls that follow its intended usage, including orderings that never occurred on-chain. We evaluate seven state-of-the-art open-weight models after one round of automated repair. Compilation success ranges from 26.4% to 92.7%, but under differential fuzzing only 31.4% of all generated function bodies that compile, pooled over models and samples, are equivalent to the original. Divergence at the contract level is the norm rather than the exception: for six of the seven models, between 13% and 31% of the generated contracts that compile diverge from the original under historical replay, and between 13% and 44% under DCR-guided replay; only Gemma-4-31B stays below 3% on both. Compilation is therefore a necessary condition for correctness and far from a sufficient one.

title: PreciseCoder: Faithful and Generalizable Debugging Beyond Unit-Test Rewards
comment: 29 pages, 14 figures
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) from unit tests is the common recipe for post-training code models, but a unit test only asks whether the final program passes. We analyze what this unit-test-only reward teaches a model during debugging and find that, while it raises pass rates, it also teaches the model to edit more and to hallucinate bugs in code that is already correct. We introduce PreciseCoder, a training algorithm that augments the unit-test reward with a signal for semantically verified, localized edits, which correlates with smaller edits and higher pass rates. On 4B, 9B, and 27B models, PreciseCoder reduces the average number of edit lines from 7-15to 3 at a pass rate on par with unit-test-only training. Trained only on single-line bugs, PreciseCoder can generalize to repository-level program repair, where it resolves more issues with smaller patches. Its precision also transfers from weaker to stronger models: given the reasoning trace of a 9B PreciseCoder model, frontier models such as GPT-5.6 Sol and Qwen3.8-Max gain 4.6-12.4 points in edit precision with no additional training. Linguistic analysis of the thinking traces shows that our reward encourages the model to reason about individual lines, name the buggy ones, and form consistent bug hypotheses.

title: SafeDSE: Joint Exploration of Safety Architecture Patterns, Mapping, and Scheduling for Dataflow Applications With Safety Arguments (Extended Version)
comment: 38 pages, 12 figures, 29 tables. Extended version of a paper submitted for publication; tool and data at github.com/SBU-CPS-Lab/SafeDSE
summary: Embedded platforms increasingly host safety-related streaming functions next to less critical ones. Whether a safety architecture pattern, such as a doer/checker pair, protects a function depends on the cores that run its components. Their schedule must meet the throughput requirement, and mixing safety integrity levels (SILs) on one core raises development cost. This report presents SafeDSE, a design space exploration framework for synchronous dataflow applications. One declarative constraint model decides the pattern of each actor, the placement that the fault model requires, the static-order schedule, and the platform, and prices SIL promotion. Guards activate the chosen patterns in a fixed graph that holds all of them, and node potentials encode throughput. An independent verifier re-checks every solution, and a generator turns its checks into evidence of a safety argument in Goal Structuring Notation. On 9 benchmark instances under period bounds, no rule that fixes patterns before mapping was both always feasible and never more expensive under conservative pricing, while joint exploration was. In the generated arguments, 49 to 62% of the leaves cite verifier checks; the rest are claims a mapping cannot discharge. Optimality within the model was proven for all synthetic graphs with up to 16 actors. This extended version adds the full model, the verifier and generator in detail, the complete catalog and parameters, and a proof of the potential characterization. It also reports every experiment per instance, a mutation analysis of the verifier, and the negative results of the development.

title: ML Engineering Agents - A Data Management Perspective
comment: 6 pages
summary: Machine learning engineering (MLE) agents are emerging as a new paradigm for automating end-to-end ML pipeline development. Using large language models for code generation and predictive performance as a machine-gradable feedback signal, these agents iteratively synthesize, execute, and refine pipeline code. Yet current systems are largely evaluated on pre-built, single-table benchmarks that abstract away key data management challenges. This tutorial introduces the foundations of MLE agents and highlights research opportunities for the database community. We cover how agents combine program synthesis with iterative and evolutionary optimization, and discuss open challenges in efficient pipeline execution, data discovery and augmentation over heterogeneous sources, reliability and debugging, as well as fairness and compliance. We connect these challenges to existing data management techniques and conclude with a hands-on session using contemporary MLE agents.

title: When Is RTL Better? Auditing Evaluation Stability with Tool-Grounded Requirement Profiles
comment: 6 pages, 3 figures, and 6 tables
summary: RTL-generation studies increasingly report functional correctness and post-synthesis quality, yet the evaluator itself is rarely treated as an experimental variable. A candidate can appear better when a security rule, protocol obligation, target context, feasibility gate, uncertainty policy, or provenance constraint is omitted. We introduce tool-grounded requirement profiles: machine-readable contracts binding each requirement's meaning to its executable evidence and comparison rule, together with cross-requirement gates, uncertainty handling, and provenance. We audit evaluator stability by freezing candidate pairs and perturbing only their evaluation profile. In a preregistered controlled pilot with six designs, twelve pairs, three requirement families, six evaluator conditions, and 72 decisions, a generic cell-count evaluator reports unsupported improvement for 6/12 pairs (50%; Wilson 95% interval 25.4 to 74.6%; design-cluster bootstrap interval 25 to 75%). The matched evaluator detects all twelve injected regressions, whereas syntax, generic synthesis, context mismatch, and gate ablation each lose the required distinction for 12/12 pairs. In a separately frozen external validation of all 290 public RTLLM v1.1 text-only candidates, 81/215 evaluable comparisons (37.7%; task-cluster 95% interval 24.8 to 51.4%) yield unsupported scalar improvements, including 72 functional-gate reversals. Separately, 26 OpenROAD-flow-scripts runs show why timing context and activity qualification must be part of the contract. The study does not rank generators; it establishes evaluator configuration as a measurable, auditable source of conclusion instability.
